All the charges against the Library were groundless and based on generalities, and a great deal of the talk about the museum was based on abysmal ignorance. (Laughter). div.head: UNPRECEDENTED SUCCESS
div.p: UNPRECEDENTED SUCCESS
INGENIOUS ARITHMETIC.

Professor C. E. Ilsoyes, of Benton Harbour, Michigan, makes use of an ingenious application of the principle that the product. of two parts is greatest when the puts aic elual, to multiply numbers of two fig,nres when their difference is not over twenty. By taking two numbers having the same sum as those whose product is required, one of which is a multiple of ten, you are able to find their product by using a multiplier with only one significant figure. This product will .vary from the desired one by the product of parts of the difference of the more remote factors sliewn by the other pair of factors, and will be that much too small if the new factors shew the greater difference, or too large if the reverse be true. To illustrate, let it be required to multiply 18 by 23. The nearest multiple of ten is 20, and 21 is the other new factor, giving a product of 420. The difference of 5 between 18 and 23 is divided by On °`. into two parts, 2 and 3, whose product, 6, must be taken from 420, giving 414, the product desired. In squaring numbers the rule becomes very simple. For example, to square 47 you multiply 50 by 44 and add the square of 3, which gives 2209. The rule see% well adapted for use by accountants, builders, and estimators where much multiplying is required.

div.head: COPPER AND WATER PURIFICATION.
div.p: COPPER AND WATER PURIFICATION.

An important discovery in the purification of contaminated water has been made by Dr. Moore and Mr. Kellerman, of the United States Depart- ment of Agriculture. It is that objectionable algw in ponds, lakelets, and storage reservoirs, ikc., can be quickly and che iply destroyed by extremely dilute solutions of copper sulphate or of metallic copper. A solution of one part copper sulphate in 100,000 of water can destroy typhoid or cholera bacteria at ordinary temperatures in three or four hours. So dilute a solution of copper is colourless, tasteless, and considered harmless to man or beast. This method is, however, not intended to supersede but to supplement the filtering method. Disagree- able tastes and odours of drinking waters are almost exclusively caused by alga., and the copper solution will prove an advantage not only for reservoirs, but pleasure ponds and lakes, fishponds, watercress beds, and so on. The copper, while killing germs of disease, does not affect harmless bacteria. A microscopical examination of the water should be made to determine the amount of copper sulphate required. No rule for this can be given. It is a matter of experience. The cost of sterilising 1,000,000 gallons of water in this way is estimated at only half a dollar or thereabouts, perhaps less.

div.head: COMPOSITION OF PORTLAND CEMENT.
div.p: THE COMPOSITION OF PORTLAND CEMENT.

In a paper presented to the American Association of Cement Manufacturers, Mr. Clifford Robinson gives the results of some researches on Portland cement. The latter consists essentially of two constituents—celite and alite. The former is a solid solution of di-calcium aluminate in di-calcium silicate, whilst alite is a solid solution of tri- calcium aluminate in tri-calcium silicate. When dry, these two constituents are in equilibrium with each other, mixing in all proportions. On the addition of water these salts are decomposed, the alite being first attacked, calcium hydrate being formed, which dissolves in the water, and the latter soon becomes supersaturated. The lime is then deposited as a network of crystals, encircling and binding together the particles not yet attacked by the water. The water, being thus freed Ll' °in its excess of lime, renews the attack on fresh particles, this being succeeded by a new deposition of lime crystals. It is the aluminates which are first attacked by the water, and it is to their decom- position that the initial setting, of the cement should be attributed, whilst the subsequent harden- ing proceeds from the gradual and much slower attack of the silicates. It has been further found that it is possible to make hydraulic cements by replacing the aluminium by iron or manganese, and the silicon by titanium, tin, lead, or even phosphorus, whilst strontium and barium may replace calcium. Some of these cements, however, prove liable to blow on setting. On the other hand, the iron cements set very slowly, but are very sound, and only a low kiln temperature is needed to produce the clinker.

div.head: BLUE LIGHT AS AN ANESTHETIC.
div.p: BLUE LIGHT AS AN ANESTHETIC.

Dr. Alfred Gradenwitz describes in the Scientific American a curious process of producing anxsthesia discovered by Professor Redard, of Geneva, and used by him for more than three years. This, Dr. Gradenwitz says, is neither a general flora local anesthesia as obtained with ancesthetic substances, insensibility being produced merely by the action of blue light on the nervous centre of vision, reacting most likely on the other nerve centres. All the experiments made by the Geneva professor go to shew that blue has a decisive amesthetic action. A great number of patients have been made unconscious by this means, and the results Nave beenyresented to the Congress of the Swiss Odontological Society. It should be mentioned that red, yellow, and other rays did not show any result, while green and violet lights most nearly related to blue light, were found to be also efficient, though to a smaller degree. The experimental outfit for this amestlietic process is a rather simple one, a 16-candle incan- descent electric lamp, a nickel-plated reflector, and a blue veil being sufficient. The lamp is fitted with a blue bulb and placed at about 6in. from the eye, this being the point,. of convergence of the light rays, while the head of the patient as also the lamp itself is covered with the blue veil to avoid any stray daylight., ! Two or three minutes' action is sufficient to allow of the extraction of a tooth without any paiii There is one poipt which apparently remains , doubtful. Professor ltedard does not state whether the person rendered unconscious by his procesb is in a state of sleep, either natural or hypnotic; but, • according to the process itself, it would seem as though there were a kind of hypnotic sleo•D• dis- appearing, however, without any prejudicial effects, Cthe moment the operation is finished and the action of the blue light discontinued, when the one experimented on seems to awake, and states that no pain has been experienced.

div.head: 8 DOCTORS AND 17 KINDS OF MEDICINE.
div.p: 8 DOCTORS AND 17 KINDS OF MEDICINE.
Bile Beans Alone Prove Beneficial.

Rarely indeed do newspaper readers come across a more remarkable statement of facts than the following, which has been made to a reporter of the "Norwich Mercury," by Mrs. James Dixon, the wife of a labourer living at Costwight, in East Norfolk. She said : "I am a Norfolk woman, and have lived in this house twelve years, and before that in another close by for twenty-live years; 'so lam well known. All my life I have _been an 'ailing woman, suffering chiefly from indigestion and biliousness. I frequently had a pain at my heart, which would suddenly, when least expected, commence to thump almost enough to take my life away. A dryness used to come into my throat at night and nearly choke me, and my husband dare not smoke in the house, as the smoke stifled me. Some months back I was of so bad colour I was convinced I was going to have jaundice. About the same time, too, I had grown to be an enormous size, and was swollen all over. Everything seemed too much ) trouble for me, and I was in so very bad .1* state I thought my children would soon lose their; mother. Almost every day I was sick, bile continuously coming up. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

I,Confirmation Service. The Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse) conducted confirmation service at the Parish Church on Saturday afternoon in the presence of a large congregation. The clergy present were the Revs. Morley Stevenson, E. J. Willcocks and T. A. J. Ridpath. One hundred and twenty candidates were presented-50 males and 70 females—the majority belonging to St. Clement's , Mission. The Bishop gave a few words of advice and encouragement to the candidates, and expressed the hope that all of them would keep the promises they had made that day, and attend communion service regularly. They must not attend the service merely as a matter of form, but in real earnest. He could not give them grace: God alone could give them that. He could only ask God to defend and help them. They had taken upon themselves the promises which had been made for them by their godfathers when they were in their childhood, and he hoped they had made the promises in the right spirit.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

Another of these pleasant meetings, was held on Sun- day last, when Mr. Joseph Oliver presided, and spoke' upon "The Brotherhood of Nan." Men should be brothers ever ready to forgive each other, sympathise,. and always ready to bear a brother's burden. Mr. Hanson of Manchester was the speaker, and followed in the thenehts and effects of brotherhood, and the great helpfulness of the P.S.A. Societies. Their P.S.A. Moss Side Manchester had an attendance of 700 to 800 every Sunday afternoon, but they also had a P.S.A. in an off street of Deansgate, where they got together some of the lowest in Manchester. One such the other day was baptised in their Church at Moss Side. He, th, speaker, was once a professional runner, and , gambler. Another P.S.A. speaker, whn had just passed away, was a converted Publican, who had given up all for Christ and now gained eternal life. Men in the lowest depths of sin, at P.S.A. meetings have been brought to Christ, and made useful men in the Church, for God and man. Said he, let us live lives of usefulness,and helpfulness to our fellow-men. Rev. J Yonge the president, and Mr. D. Owen took part in the meeting. The Secretary welcomed three new members There are 441 now enrolled. Six new members joined the Sick Club. A vote of sympathy was passed to Mr. Taker and his family, who have recently sustained a bereavement.

SALF,ORD " A " v. WARRINGTON "A." , These teams played their return match at Salford on ' Saturday. The visitors were soon on the attack, as the result of capital passing, and both Davies and Brooks almost crossed. Knight was at fault in taking some tall returns,and the venue was changed. Salford became especi- ally dangerous when Bate was tackled in possession, but Davies eventually got his side:out of a difficult corrier.The Warringtonians excelled in some back play, and Brooks, takinn, a pass from Davies,scored brilliantly,Knight add- ing die goal. Berry was responsible for the"Wirepullers" maintaining the aggressive, but eventually Salford with a good spurt, reached the Warrington quarter flag. The stay here, however, was of the briefest description, for effective runs by Berry and Brooks placed the visitors in a strong position. The tackling of Salford was sound, and McWhirter made a hold attempt for the home side, Knight effecting a fine tackle. Riley failed at a penalty,[and Jordan ran the ball out to centres field, when the interval arrived with the score of one gal and one try (five points) in Warrington's favour. On resuming the visitors immediately gained the upper hand and splendid combination let to Jordan scoring fine try. This was the only score. Warringtoa thus achieving victory by one goal two tries (eight points) to nil.

LATCHFORD STEEL WORKS V. RUNCORN RRSERVES. About 600 spectators assembled to see this encounter at Latchford on Saturday. The Steel Works started, and Moran made a splendid run for Latchford, his attempts to score being defeated by the Runcorn halves. Runcorn were awarded a free kick, and made headway. Latchford got away again, but Lowndes missed the leather, and after a little midfield play, Runcorn com- bined splendidly, and were eventually, awarded a free kick, R. Brown placing a goal. Half -time : Runcorn, two points •, Latchford Steel Works, nil. After the interval the Works assumed the aggressive, and Knight made an attempt to score from a passing bout. Johnson dropped a fine goal. Latchford attacked, and found touch nicely. Runcorn again got possession, end E. Houghton landed another goal with a fine drop. The Reserves won by six points to nil.

A COLLIER'S BRUTALITY. • At'St. Helens, on Tuesday, Daniel Lilly, a collier was charged with assault, having, it was alleged almos bitten the nose off James Greenall, his brother-in-law Greenall said that on Saturday night, after walking home together, prisoner set into him with his feet and made his head like a lump of jelly. He also got him down under the table and got bold of his nose in his teeth and bit the end off.—William Greenall, complain- ant's brother, said that prisoner threatened all the any home that " someone was going to be laid out."—The magistrates sent Lilly to gaol for a month.

Warrington were at home again on Saturday their -opponents being Salford. Both sides were strongly represented, llockenhlll turning out for the horuesters after an absence of two months,and receiving a flattering reception. Fine weather prevailed and a crowd of about 4,000 assembled. Mr. F. Kennedy of Broughton, was the referee and the teams lined out as follows : Warrington—Hallam, back; Fish,lsherwood, Dicken- son and Kenyon, three-quarter backs; D. Davies and Hockenhall, half backs ; Preston, Shngars, Boardman, Jolley, Swift, Belton. Cook, and Thomas, forwards. ,Salford—Lambert,.back •' Bell, Thomas, Lomas, and Richards three-quarter backs; Preston and John, half backs; Rhapps, Rees, Lewis, Spencer, Brown, Williams, Buckler and Warwick, forwards. Touch judges, Messrs. F. Hancock, Runcorn, and J. H. Sansom, Leigh. The game opened in favour of the home side, and passing between Ilockenhall, Davies, and Fish took Play direct to the Salford line. Here some fine defen- sive work was exhibited by Lomas and Lambert. and following a scart clearance by the Salford custodian, John gave Hallam trouble with an effective run. Isher- wood and Kenyon beat off the attack, and Lamhert. in trying to take a return from Hallam, fractured the cap .of the right knee, and took no further pin in the game. Warrington maintained the pressure, and the visitors 'being penalised, Preston placed a goal. Salford responded gamely, and Kenyon only just succeeded in :stopping Lomas near the Warrington line. Isherwood broke away finely with Fish in attendance but the wing man spoiled the movement by getting in 'front of his -centre and taking a pass forward. Half-time arrived With Warrington leading by a goal to nil. On resuming, the home side appeared to take matters rather easily and Salford frequently attacked. Lomas followed up a short punt by John and was only robbed by Dickinson-ha close proximity to the posts. Towards the close, the home vanguard did some earnest work and Salford were forced to the line. Kenyon was tackled at the corner after smart passing, but a moment later, D. Davies feinted cleverly and dodged over the line. Preston failed at goal and the game shortly ended with Warrington winning by 1 goal. 1 try (5 points) to 'Salford nil.

WARRINGTON WIN AT WIDNES. Warrington's return match with Widnes, postponed from April Ist, took place on Monday evening at Widnes in fine but dull weather. The kick-off was at 6 o'clock -and there was a gate of about 2,500, a third of whom 'came from Warrington. Both sides had changes from Saturday's teams, but the fifteens were representative. •Widnes Tilley, back ; Hughes, Taylor, Peacock, and Wailing, three-quarter backs ; Lally and Morris, half backs , • Cockrum McDonald, McCabe, Webster, Turner,

Lee,-A'spey, and McCarthy, forwards. Warrington—Hallam, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son, and Kenyon, three-quarter backs • Hockenhall and Brooks, half backs ; Boardman, Thomas, Morrison, Harmer, Jolley, Swift, Preston, and Belton, forwards. Referee, Mr. Kennedy (Broughton) •, touch judges, Messrs. Jones (Runcorn) and Houghton (St. Helms). Aspey started for Widnes, who at once rushed the game to the Warrington quarter. Fish relieved with a tricky run to centre where McCabe and be collided,both requiring a brief rest in consequence. Peacock retali- ated with aron into the Warrington half, Kenyon marking nicely. A penalty gave Warrington relief, and Isherwood running well punted to Tilley. The home full back misjudged the ball,and Swift securing. posses- sion ran in an easy try, which Fish failed to improve °Ton. The Widnesians rallied strongly and forced NVarrington to the line Hughes nearly getting •ever after a strong run by Ike Taylor. Hallam cleared brilliantly and put Warrington on the attack again. A line pica of work by Isherwood, Dickenson and Kenyon resulted in the latter running strongly and kicking past Tilley for Isherwood to score a try. Fish kicked a goal. Ilalf-time was now near at hand, but before the interval henyon made another grand run which terminated a 'yard from the line. \Farrington 8 points, Widnes nil. Preston resumed with a powerful kick which Lally rnisfielded near the line. Widnes gradually raised the siege, and smart passing by Lally, Peacock and Taylor looked like taking the ball well into the Warrington half, when Fish intercepted at centre. He was off like a shot, and outpacing Lally scored brilliantly near the •corner, Preston making a poor attempt at goal. The home team responded gamely and rushed the ball to the IVarrington lino. Scrambling play followed in which Lally scored by a determined rush, Tilley failing at goal. liockenhall broke away brilliantly and after parting with -the ball he was charged over with the unfortunate result that his collar-bone was broken for the second time this
C

year, and he retired from the game. Thomas filled the vacancy and passed to Isherwood close in, the latter dropping a goal very smartly. As before, Widnes responded vigorously and Hughes nearly got in at the right corner. Isherwood returned with a long point which Hughes failed to gather, and Thomas dashing up scored a good try which Fish improved upon. One more effort by Widnes followed, and a misunderstanding by the Warrington backs let in Mc earthy who dashed over with a try. Final score: Warrington, 3 goals, 4 tries, 18 points ; Widnes, 2 tries, 6 points. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. BRADFORD. Played at Hull, on Monday, both sides being strongly represented, Eagers, Turner and Dimbsvin scored for Bradford, and West for Hull. Result :—Bradford 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points) to Kingston Rovers 1 goal and 1 try (5 points).

The woman's face brightened. " I do not understand you, Jack," she said. " How did she die? Why do you say that you have killed her ? " " She died a natural death," he replied. " She died of a broken heart." A sudden look of fury came into the woman's face, but it passed as quickly as it came. She grew very white and her lips were pressed closely together. She understood. Both were silent for quite a minute. Then Marie de la Mothe came up to him and laid Due hand upon his arm. " Jack," she whispered, "you are free." "I am free," he replied, mechanically, "Why do you say the worst has hap- pened I" He was silent. "How can. it be the worst when you are free," she contmueud. " You did not love your wife, and she—you have often told me of your home life." She looked up into his fac'e pleadingly. But he dared not meet her eyes, and he stared fixedly at the window. He had resolved that nothing should turn him from his purpose. Yet he could not bring himself to say that which had to be said. "Why do you not answer," she murmured. F' Are you not glad that you are free? " Last night's scene flail-led across his brain— the figure in the chair, the awful silence, the a,,cl the marked passage on it! tear-stained page. Glad 1 Oh, God, the mockery Of it all. He clenched his hands and walked away to the window. Then he came back to Marie de la Mothe, who, faced him with flashing eyes. The day of the funeral (was cold and bleak. A bitter wind blew from the north and drove a few scattered flakes of snow across the church- yard. John Porteous listened to the burial service with a face of stone. Not a muscle moved nor an eyelid quivered. To an ordinary spectator it would have seemed that he was merely a respectful mourner, perhaps some distant relative of the deceased, who had been left some money, and who had attended the funeral as a forrnal mark of respect. The little boy stood by his side with a irightened look in his large grey eyes. He barely understood what had happened, but his childish mind was terrified at the solemnity find gloom of the proceedings. It was only when the coffin had been towered into the grave, and Porteous had taken a last look at it before the earth had overed it up, that he showed any sigtis of !motion, and lifting his child up in his arms, ne kissed him. No one guessed that he meant that kiss for his dead wife, and that it sealed the i7CseAution of atonement.

at least to me woman wno was aeaa, too woman he had once loved, the woman who had died through his hand.. . .

Yet sentim-ent would have to be thrust aside if he was to escape the clutches of the law. Sentiment would not weigh with the bank, and the discovery was the matter of a few days, perhaps of a few hours. He could replace nearly £4,500, but. the £6,800 had gone as surely as though the money lay at the bottom of the sea. It was the price he had paid for his infidelity, and he had not even yet received that which he had bought. The whole situation was dark and horrible. He could not turn back. It was impossible to go forward. Yet to stand still meant exposure, disgrace, imprisonment—perhaps a long term of penal servitude, for the law does not deal kindly with a man of high position who has abused his trust.

All through the night he sat in his chair, and tried to think of some way out of the difficulties that beset him. But his thoughts were clouded by the dark shadow that had crept into the room, and he found it impossible to reason out any clear plan of action. He could not forget what he had seen by the desk. Every scheme for the future faded into darkness, where nothing could be distinguished but the silent figure with bowed head and folded arms, and through the silence rang the music of a single refrain : _ . .

" Believe me- if all these enduring young charms That I gaze on so fondly to-day." The significance. of the words was terrible. Every note of the music was a pang ;that wrung nerve, and heart, and brain. Only once did he rise from his chair through all that long and terrible night ; then with a sudden impulse he. crossed over to the desk, and, unlocking one of the drawers, took out a revolver. For some minutes he stood irreso- lute. He did not fear death, but he feated the imputation of cowardice which " death would bring. A fierce battle .raged in his mind. With a set purpose he kept his eyes on the spot where his wife had died. He intensified the horror of his position by every means in in his power, by every thought that would bring home to him the necessity of death. Thrice he raised the weapon to his forehead, and thrice his arm sunk slowly back to his side. The photograph of his only son stood on his desk and he could not keep his eyes off it. The. baby face laughed at him across the misty flood which swain before his eyes: Yet it was like the-face of an accusing' angel, and he saw it age with misery and despair, and he heard a voice crying out, " •1 am the son of a felon and a suicide." Finally, he thrust the revolver back into the drawer, and crossing over . to the fireplace, flung him- self into a chair.

When dawn broke,his eyes were closed in a brief sleep, and his white and haggard face looked horrible in the grey morning light. One of the servants found him there, and the noise of her footsteps roused him from his slumber. Another day had broken, and the light was more terrible than the darkness had been.

He stumbled upstairs, shaved, had a cold bath, and changed his clothes. The ordinary duties of civilised la in some measure re- stored him to ,his senses. He, ate a poor breakfast, lit a cigar, and drove round to the bank. He reflected in an agony of shame that a real 'excuse for absence now lay ready to his hand.

From there he • drove to the house of Marie de la Mothe. He had ohly one clear idea for the future in his mind, that he must break-all the chains that bound him to this woman. He owed that at least to his dead wife. He was now free to marry whom he chose. The bonds that he had found so irksome had been cut once and for all. .Yet the memory of them had become stronger than the reality had ever been. He felt . that it was now impossible for him to Marry this woman. He had killed his wife by his neglect. This was the least atone- ment he .could.make for his crime.

With this idea strong in his mind, he rang the bell of 46, Carey Terrace, and was shown int 9 the drawing-room. The maid lit the fire and went to find her mistress. In a minute or two she brought back word that Mrs. de la Mothe would see him in about half an hour, if he cared to wait. He nodded 'assent, - He did‘ not care to wait, but it, was necessary for him to do so. He. required all his strength for the battle that lay before • him, a battle not only with the woman who loved him, but with his own passions and desires. Every moment of delay was against him. His purpose was firm and unalterable. But as each minute passed he realised more and more how hard he would have to fight for victory. The very room was antagonistic to his purpose. The little presents he had given this woman were dotted about on tables and shelves. Each one of them recalled some tender memdry. In an hour's time Marie de la Mothe ap- peared. She looked radiantly beautiful, and had evidently spared no time nor trouble over lye toilet. She was, as usual, half an hour late. As a rule he chaffed her about her unpunctuality, but to-day he rose to his feet and took her hand in silence. His face was white and haggard. She glanced at him un- easily. She could see at once that his manner towards her had changed. "What has happened ?" she said abruptly. "The worst," he replied, not daring to look ner.straight in the lace. _ . _

" The Bank," she cried, laying hold of his arm. " Impossible ! You told me twenty. four hours at least—and why are you here; why are you not—? " " It is not the Bank, Marie," he said in a low voice. She loose,cl his arm and looked keenly into his face. r• "Not the Bank," she exclaimed, "what is it then? Why doyoSis look away from me? 'What is it? Something you are afraid to tell me ? " _ . .

"I have come to say good-bye. Marie," he replied," I may not see you again. Her face grew pale. Her eyes flashed dan- gerously and she laughed. VA." Good-bye," she repeated. "Yes, yes, of course," she added nervously. " How you frightened me. You go to-morrow, hut in a month's time—you silly old Jack, it is only a month after all," and she clung lovingly to his shoulder. _ . _ _

" It is for longer than that, Marie," he said slowly. Then he swung round sharply and her hands dropped from his shoulder. " What has happened ? " she cried. "My wife is dead," he answered in a kw voice. ' .

"Your wife ? . Dead ? " she repeated, "you have not—" And she shrank from him with a look of horror. " I hate killed her." he said in a hard voice, " you may well shrink from me. In the eyes of the law lam not a murderer. But I have killed her, as surely as if I_ltad- shot or poi- soned her." _

I quietly, "that it has removed the only Dar- tier to our marriage." I "Do you not understand? "he continued. I scarcely heeding her interruption. "Well. I will try and make it clear to you," and he told her briefly the story of the night before. She listened almost, as it seemed, impassive- ly, for one whose whole fate was bound up in the narrative. When he had finished, she laughed. . ' I uriderstand," she said, "you miserable coward I You do not love Inc. You have been acting • a lie. You have—bah I why should I talk of it. You have made the first excuse that came ready to your hand. It is a poor one, Jack, a very poor one. And I—" She sank into a chair, and burying her face in her hands, sobbed passionately. .„ He came to her side and laid his hand upon her shoulder. The steugele within him was terrible. Well he knew that if he lost, his whole life would be too ghastly to endure. He knew that the memory c.f the night before would hold him to the day of his death. " Marie," he said tend,rly, j " I love you still. But—but this has risen between us. I love you, and it is that which will be nay punishment. I have much to atone for, and then there is my child." She did not look up, but her whole body was sfaelien with sobs. "My child is motherless," he continued. " I have wronged him enough already. I cannot leave England lentil my wife is buried. And any moreent / ,may be arrested. j• He is the snri of a thief." " Why do yolf not leave to-morrow, and tako him with yon," sbe broke in; raising a tear-stained face from her harvls. " I cannot go until my wife is buried," he said doggedly. "Why not? " " I cannot go," he renerited. " You mean, yon Vs El not ? " "I cannot el," he said sternly, "I have some decency left in me." She came close up to him and grasped him by the arm. " You must go," she said slowly. " I intend to stay." Ho had made up' his mind on this point, and nothing could move him now. If by going he could have saved his child from shame he would have, perhaps, yielded. But it was merely a question of bis own punishment. Whether he paid the penalty of his crime, or escaped from justice. Ids child's position would be the same. He would be the son of a com- mon felon. - For his own sake it would be best to go. But he thrust all thought -of self aside. " I intend to stay." he repeated. " I have made my plans. The funeral will take place in three days' time. It is possible I shall not be found out for a week. Directly the funeral is over I shall leave England." " Alone ? " the woman said, in a tender voice.. „ "With my child." His voice trembled, and the woman was quick • to notice his emotion. Without a word she flung her arms about his neck, and burst into tears. . "Marie, Marie,"/he whispered, "it is not because Ido not love you that Ido this. I was ready to give up everything for you, to leave my wife, to sacrifice my honour. But what has happened has risen between us like a cloud. It isbetter for both of us to part.. We can never be happy with this shadow upon us. . I am .a murderer, and I have killed a woman who loved me." " Not as I love you," she cried, seizing his left hand in hers. Do you remember when I gave you this ring? " It was a single large opal in a plain gold setting. He wore it on his third finger. j He. remembered well when she had given it to him. He had sworn I 'ever to take it from his hand, and to love her ..o the day of his death. " I remember," he said solemnly, "and I ' will wear it always. But after to-day I will never see you again." She broke away from his clasp and faced him with flushed cheeks and eyes that blazed through their hot tears. " )iou can go," she cried. He stood irre- solute. "Go. I tell you," she repeated. • "You cur," and she pointed to the door. He raised his eyes and read the truth in her face. Her love had turned to the fierce hatred of a woman 'who had been scorned. He moved towards the -door. When he reached it, he stood for a moment irresolute. The woman held her breath, and stared at him with parted lips. If he would only come back to her, and kiss her, and say good-bye, she might yet move him from his ,purpose. But j Jack Porteous knew how weak he was in this' ' woman's hands. • " Good-bye, Marie," he said in a low voice. He did not even turn his heart. He was afraid, and slunk out of the door like a beaten hound. Marie de la .Mothe moved a step forward and words of entreaty were on her laps. But in a moment she stamped out this last spark of love, and walking over to the fireplace, rang the bell. A minute later she heard the hall door close. She went to the window and watched the tall figure walk down the street. He did not look back. Then a sudden burst of fury seized her. She picked up a gold and tortoiseshell paper- knife and breaking it in half, threw the pieces in the fire. .It had been a gift from her lover. Then she tore the pearl necklace from her throat and stamped it under her foot. Then she moved round the room slowly and deliber- ately, and seizing everything he had ever given her, she dashed -them one after the other into the fireplace: and beat them int 6 shapeless and broken debris with a poker. Then she flung herself on the sofa, and lay there with a white face and tearless eyes, staring at the fire until the whole room seemed bathed with blood-red flames. Then sudden- ly she rose to her feet and laughed. An idea had come to her. " He shall suffer for this," she cried aloud "My God I how he shall suffer."
CHAPTER IV.

A WOMAN'S VENGEANCE. FORTUNE favoured Jack Porteous during the next two days, and all his arrangements for leaving the country were carried out satisfactorily. Three hours after he had left Marie de la Mothe, he discovered that it was practically certain his defalcations would not be dis- covered for at least a fortnight, and the terrox of immediate detection was removed. He was also lucky in being able to transfer his. berth on the " Oroguoya " t. a steamer sail- ing the next week. But the otiestion of his child presented many difficulties. He had to decide Nviien.ct to take the boy with him or leave him behind in the care of some relatives. It was a hard struggle for the wretched man. He was devoted to his son, and he reslisee. that if they parted at all the parting would have to be for ever. He could rot claim the child in after years and brand hint with hi-, Lther's shame. For a nhnle night he fought out a lient battle with himself. It was the night before his wife's funeral. Her body lay in the next room. The lid of the coffin had been screwed down and he hnew that he could never see her face. again.. But that face still lived in the features of her child.

All night he lay awake and stared into the darkness. But when the cold grey light of morning came he had made up his mind. His atonement had to be final and complete. His Own feelings had to be sacrificed. The child must never see its father again, must never even know its father's name.

div.head: By J. B. HARRIS BURLANA
div.p: By J. B. HARRIS BURLANA
CHAPTER H.—ContznuedJ

He found his latch key and lit a match, sheltering it with his hand. Something brushed against his feet, and, looking down he saw a blotched mass of fur, and heard the iiaint mew of a cat. He kicked, out with all his force, and the wretched animal rolled screaming clown the steps. He put the key into the lock and opened the door. But once again the fear of some un- known evil seized him, and he. clung Ito the side of the doorway, his teeth chattering with terror. He cursed himself' for a fool, and staggering into the hall, closed the door behind him. A single spot of light glowed above his head. It was the hall lamp turned down to a mere speck of flame. He reached up a trembling hand, fumbled for a few minutes with the tap, and finally succeeded in extinguishing the light. He reeled back against the wall, and the perspiration streamed from every pore in his body. It seemed to ,him hours since he had seen the light. He listened attentively and thought he heard something move far up on one of the landings. The clock in the hall ticked loudly, and the beating of his heart seemed to keep time with it. He idly won- dered what would happen if the clock sud- denly stopped. He opened his lips to call out. He had often crept quietly upstairs after returning from his club, so that his wife should not wake and upbraid him with a bitter tongue. He now longed to hear her voice as he stood there in the darkness.' He moved forward, and purposely stumbled in the hope of rousing here The noise echoed through the house, and he waited eagerly for a door to open on the land- ing above. But nothing stirred. Then he pulled himself together, and, striking a match, looked carefully rOund as' though he expected to see something. At the far end Of ithe hall the movement of a dim figure caught his eye. Then he laughed, for he saw that the figure also held a light, and was merely his own reflection in the looking- glass. He realised the absurdity of his terror, mid, reaching up his hand, turned on the gas and put a match to it. In a moment the hall was flooded with light, and fear, to a large extent, vanished with the darkness. He lit a candle which Stood on the hall table and began to ascend the stairs. Then he suddenly recollected the letter to the bank, and, retracing his steps, crossed the ball, went down a short passage, and opened the door of his study. As he entered a cold draught of air swept across the room, and blew out the candle. He heard a rastling of some papers as they fluttered to the floor, and he stariel nervously at the sound. Tile hall lamp was hidden by the angle of the passage. and only, a faint, reflected light stole through the open door. He could, how- ever, just see the table in the centre of the room, and, moving forward, he placed the candlestick upon it, while. he felt in his pocket for another match. Then he remembered the draught, and, making his way back to the door, closed it. The room was now in absolute darkness. Something rustled by the window. . ,

. , He found his match-box and struck a light. Then he gave a start of surprise. Someone waS sitting at his desk by the window. It was a woman with her head sunk forward in her arms. He lit the candle and advanced towards the silent figure. It was his wife. She was apparently asleep, for she did not move.

For a momena, he stood in hesitation. He thought of the 'proverb, "Let sleeping dogs lie." If he roused his wife he knew what he might expect to hear from her lips. Yet he could scarcely with decency leave her there until she awoke of her own accord. He resolved to write and post his letter to the bank.. Then he could wake her from her sleep. and go off to bed before she thoroughly realised who had roused her.

He walked up tip-toe to the desk, and took the inkpot and a pen over to the table. As he did so his hand touched one of the silver candle- sticks. It was still hot. The candle had burned down to the socket. He looked round for some writing-paper. There was none to be seen, !Mt he knew that there was plenty in the second drawer from the top on the left hand side of the desk. , '

He sank quietly on one knee, and opened the drawer. His. head was close to his wife's shoulder. He took out a sheet of paper and an envelope. Then for the first time he noticed the cOmplete silence. He held his breath and listened. .There was not a single sound ht the beating of his own heart. A sudden fear seized him. He tried to see his wife's face. It was buried in her arms. He rose suddenly to his feet, and, taking the candle from .the table, thrust it close to her and scrutinised her narrowly. She was absolutely still. There was no movement or sound of breathing.

div.head: CHAPTER 111.
div.p: CHAPTER 111.
THE BREAKING OF THE CHAIN.

No one answered the bell in response to Porteous' summons. It was now 2.30, and the servants were fast asleep at the top of the house. With an effort the man roused him- self to action. Staggering to his feet, he left the room, passed out of the hall door, and groped his way through the fog to the nearest doctor.

The two men returned together. The doctor pronounced life to be extinct. He had attended Mrs. Porteous before and said he knew her heart was weak. Death was due to syncope. Did her husband know of anything that would have been likely to give a great shock to her system? Porteous replied mechanically that he was not aware of anything of the sort. He said nothing of the life the two had led for the last three years—the endless quarrels, the sullen endurance of each other's society, the mu.tua, neglect, the indifference, growing gradually into positive hatred. All this would have had but little effect on a hard and callous woman, such as he had imagined his wife to be. But in the last hour his eyes had been opened to the terrible truth. She had loved him to the last. She had, perhaps, through ail these years, battled in vain with her own unhappy temperament and lived in the hope of regaining her husband's love. His mind went swiftly over the past and he thought he could now recall certain half-hearted ad- vances on her part; advances made with genuine hope of reconciliation, but so subdued by the sense of wrongs she had suffered that they were scarcely more than a faint intima- tion of the spirit that prompted them. Such a life must have been a hell to a woman whc loved, and who yet was unable to overcome her sense of resentment. Such a life might well kill a woman with a weak heart. And John Porteous did not look ihe doctor in the face,when he told him that he knew of nothing that could have caused her death. The servants were roused, and Mrs Porteous was carried to her bedroom. The doctor left, and Porteous stayed on alone in the study. He lit a dozen candles and made the room a blaze of light. Then he fetched sticks and paper from the kitchen and re-lit the fire. It blazed up cheerfully with the aid of a little lamp oil, and in less than an hour the room had assumed a more comfortable aspect. But to John Porteous the darkness and Cold still lay upon it. The thin veil of fog still hung over everything, and in the :hair by the desk still sat the shadow of death. He crouched close to the fire for warmth. He turned his back upon the window. There was much to be thought of that night, much even to be done. The hand of God had struck, and had struck hard. The blow had fallen in the very centre of his dishonourable plans and ecattered them in pieces to the four winds of Heaven. He had robbed the bank and could not repay the money. His wife was dead, and he could not leave England until she had been buried. Then there was the boy. It would be impossible to desert a motherless and helpless child. Yet his pas- sage was taken on the " Oroquoya," and Marie de la Mothe—he clenched his hands in agony. But out of the chaos of his thoughts came one single idea, clear cut and definite. He could not marry Marie de la Mothe. He owed that

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
APRIL 15th. 1905.
THE Budget is a THE BUDGET AND THE mild and harmless INCOME TAX. exercise by a

financier without originality. With his surplus Mr. AUSTIN CHAMBERLAIN: was plainly unable to give relief to the income tax payers. He has chosen to take off tea the extra twopence he imposed last year. This procedure is perfectly correct, but will not excite enthusiasm. There is nothing in the Budget to revive the drooping hopes of Unionists throughout the country. They can only be thankful that it does not excite irritation, and will not land the Chancellor of the Exchequer in such a mess as he was last yeir with the tobacco duty. It was impossible to take off the income tax, bemuse a penny is equivalent to £2,200,000, which the CHANCELLOR could not spare. Tea is a food of the people, though we are not sure that the increased consumption which may follow the remission of taxation will prove an unmixed benefit. With many woman tea-drinking is really a form of dram-drinking, and does as much harm to the nervous system. A noteworthy point in the Budget speech marks the decline of the yield from excise. There is a great diminution in the consumption of beer wines and spirits. Mr. AI7iTEN CHAMBERLAIN spoke somewhat mournfully of this, strictly from a Chancellor of the Exchequer's point of view. But apart from professional considerations he recog- nised it as a salutary change in the habits of the

people. It creates, however, a new problem of national finance. There is a steady decline in the drink bill, and if it should continue the custodians of the national purse will have to make the deficiency good by fresh taxation. This is the sort of omergency to which a financer of Mr. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN'S calibre is not equal. Originality needed, and also courage. Anybody could pot

twopence on the tea duty one year and take it off the next. But a thorough re-organisation of the finances require a bolder heart. The yield from the income'tax has exceeded the estimate by a million and a quarter. Mr. Ausren7 CHAMBERLAIN drily observed that he has not reckoned with the efficiency of the collection. It is not very probable that he will introduce another Budget, so he will enjoy the reputation of having left the income tax at a shilling in the pound in time of peace. Unless the revenue of the corning year should greatly exceed the estimate there is no prospect that this tax will be reduced in. the next Budget by more than a penny, if at all. Whenever the revenue loses its elasticity, the income tax is the chief resource of the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer,and it is:as likely as not tha • a penny taken off next year will be put on again the year after. There is a manifest likelihood, therefore,that the tax will seldom if ever fall below a shilling, and will continue to press with increas- ing hardship on the class that can least afford it. The principle of a graduated income tax has been freely denounced by men of both parties, but without any convincing demonstration. By abatements on.,incomes below a certain figure, the principle has already been recognised, and the question now relates not to its adoption but to its extended application. If it is right to grant abatements, there can be nothing immoral in varying the incidence of the tax so as to make large,permatient incomes pay on a higher scale than Bai.lll and fluctuating incomes

If a man has ten thousand a year from inhErited and assured investments, why should be not pay something more in the pound than the man who has a thousand a year entirely ,depeudent on his capacity to earn it ? This is a view which has Mr. JosErnCHANtanuLAlN's sympathy in the days when he preached the doctrine of "ransom." Ransom is not a pretty word. Equity is better, and we should say it was decidedly equitable to levy taxa- tion in proportion to th 9 size of the income, and to its stability. But for a reform of this character we need a Chancellor of the Exchequer with a good deal more backbone than Mr. AUSTEN CHAMBER: LAIN possesses, and very different political associations.

The Liberal organization under the astute and active leadership of Mr. Howes is not letting the grass grow under its feet. Every opportur.ity is being taken to educate the constituency no to the pressing requirements of the hour, and the voter who does not, by this, know all about the defici- encies and delinquencies of the • present Govern- ment must be either apathetic or wooden-headed. During the week Liberal meetings have been held in different parts of the town, and the speeches of such men as Councillor Middletor' of Gramm, Mr. Henry Vivian, Liberal candidate for Birkenhead? and Mr. Fred Maddison, Liberal and Labour candidate for Burnley, have done much to expand the enthusiasm of the stalwarts and clinch the opinions of the waverers. The speech by Mr. Vivian at Wednesday evening's meeting made a great impression. Workingmen always like to listen to those who by experience are able to sympathise with them and speak from their point of view, and Mr. V.vian could assure his hearers th...t: as a worker he was a member of the Joiners' and Carpenters' Society and could produce his "ticket." He is a hard hitter and his unsparing denunication of Protection, backed up by powerful arguments, had an inspiring effect. The confidence of Warrington Liberals in the ulti- mate issue grows daily, while the Conservatives appear to be sinking rapidly from dejection to despair. They arei n for a licking this time and they know it. A arge percentage of the electors like to be on the winning side, and this floating vote is sure to be cast for the Progressive party and Warrington gives ample indications of follow• ing the magnificent lead of Bute, Bury, and Brighton.

Our congratulations to Alderman Tinnion ! lie obtained his promotion in the Council on Tuesday and though the margin of votes in his favour was only small, few will deny that he has well-earned the honour. During the ten years he has bowl a representative for S. Austin's Ward, Mr. Tinnion has devoted an amount of time and labour to the service of the ratepayers which is altogether out of the ordinary. He is a member of no less than eight committees and takes an active part in their deliberations. The Paving and Sewerage Committee—one of the most important of committees—owns in him an exemplary chairman, while in the Council itself the new Alderman's grasp of affairs has always been apparent. We nope he will be fortunate enough to equal the splendid record of his pre- decessor, the late Alderman Sutton, with 31 years service in the Corporation of Warringtcri.

For some years now, politics have not intruded much into the Council Chamber. Aldermauic elections have been settled by virtue of seuority, and the peacefulness of the method has un- doubtedly tended to smoother and more efficient local administration. On Tuesday, however, the senority rule, to which nearly all the members of the Council are pledged by signature, was rudely broken. Not that Alderman Tinnion was not the senior Councillor. He and Councillors Ellison and Duncan are on level terms with nearly ten years' service each, but the candidature of Councillor John Roberts in opposition to Alderman Tinnion

scattered the sacredness of seniority to the winds. The Conservatives apparently took fright at the prospect of a succession of senior Liberals, and in obedience to the crack of the party whip they left their pledges with their con- sciences—at home. Seeing that Concillor Ti onion and the other Liberals have always observed the contract as binding in the election of Tory Alder- men, the sudden revolt of the Tories savoured very much of both political and personal treachery. Three of them, the Mayor, Alderman Evans, and Alderman Bennett voted straight, while Aldermen Smethurst and !Hutchinson abstained from voting. To these men all honour is doe for placing principle before party. Alderman Tinnion had a narrow escape, but he is entitled to additional satisfaction from the fact that, notwith- standing a surprise attack, he triumphed. There are now two Liberal aldermen out of nine, but if the elections both in and out of the Council are in future to be fought politically there is good reason to expect a more equitable adjustment of the balance of power before very long.

The election of Mr. Henry Roberts to the Education Committee is an interesting event for the reason that it marks the return to public life in a tentative way of the man who voluntarily relinquished his offices under the Corporation as a result of the Non-Trading agitation. Councillor Lord voiced the view of the Non-Traders when he said that if Mr. Roberts would give an undertaking that the firm in which he and his family were largely interested would not trade through that Committee with the Corporation they would not object to his election. It was perhaps too much to expect any such declaration from Mr. Roberts, but we hope he will see the expediency, while he is a member of the Education Committee of refraining from all trading through the NVar- rington Slate Company with the Committee. This much is, we think, due in deference to the public

div.p: opinion so unmistakably expressed during the agitation. In other respects, Mr, R 'hefts will no doubt prove a valuable wernber of the authority.

Warrington Town Council will soon be famous for its " inquiries." Apparently, the Angean stables have not yet been ewept perfectly clean. At the meeting a month ago, it Will be remembered, Alderman Tinnion made a remarkable statement to the effect that he had been told circumstanti- ally of a member of the Council attempting to BO use his position as to benefit to the extent of £lOO. No names were mentioned, though Mr. Tinnion would have been privileged to state all he knew. The matter is not to rest where it stands, however. A resolntion authorising a committee of investigation was passed on the motion of Councillor Lprd, and presumably we shall learn in con-se of time what really did transpire between two men in a train If they are willing to tell us I It is rumoured that this is not the only charge of attempted misuse of public confidence, and that the committee of iuvestigat;cn wiil be given wide Powers. The honour of the Council and its members is involved and we hope that no effort will be spared to arrive at the truth in this unpleasant affair.

The Budget was the least interesting item dis- cussed, owing to the faCt that the partictilwa of it, and the or, spertive reduction of the rates, were Published st night ago. Like the Ctfancollur of the national Eretequer, Al&rman yery simple, understandable statement to sub- mit, and his announcement of a t%vopeney reduc. tioa in the rates was received with as little emotion as was Mr. Austen Cnamberlain's abatement of twopence on the tea duty. Alderman Bennett took advantage of the Couricirs philosophic content to press the claims of the branch library scheme, and we were very glad to note that the Council con- sented to the re-introduction of the modest £2OO reqnired, into the estimates. Seeing that the venture was sanctioned two years ago, and considering the small expend,ture it would have been paltry in the extreme for the 'Council to have deleted the item horn the estimates stelond time. The project of placing extended r,"•ditie• facilities within easier reach of the public LS a tVllitarir.tm experiment which will be watched With hopeful interest. •

The movement in fsvour of the opening of !Pecial Courts for the hearing of cases against Juvenile offenders appears to be gaining ground. :Birmingham has now adopted the innovation, sud we note that it was explained that the magistrates Were anxious to keep children apart from the evil earroundings of the cullnary police court, and to deal with them in a correctional rather than a Penal manner, with the object that crime might be checked in the earliest stax,es instead of punishing it When it had arrived at the flood. In Warring- -oth happily, we are not troubled with so many cuarges against javeuiles as the magistrates Ire eilmpelled to deal with, in larger towns, bu still occasiol'. do arise whim children have to answer for their misdeeds before the Bench. There is Inuch to commend the idea of dealing with sir:ll se"es apart from the ordinary Police business, and hile the holding Of akpecial court regularly is hardly justified, we would suggest the use of tho ..oroner's Court tor the purpose when necessity Beroandi.

: Heywood has been experi-nentin in the dime- " 4'"" of providing municipal entertainments for the towuspoople. Sixteen concerts held during the past seivain were evidently much appreciated ae the attendances totalled 11,025. Taere WHS. 11.,"wer, a small loss on the undertalting—R2l 4. 7d. A few years ego Warrington people had the advantage of all excellent series of municipal autertaitiments, but the xpenses were heavy end, although the attendances were often large, deficit bad to be faced. The result „rlyfle that the Corporation abandoned the venture. ovi that the Council is showing a marked disposi- ttion to consider the intellectual profit of the. nwnsPeople by sanctioning such worthy improve- Monts as branch libraries, it migiithe worth while tc.io take the entertainment scheme in hand again. Sufficient public support would perhaps be forth• to produce a satisfactory financial result, but even if there were a small loss it would, in our he justified by the placing of first-class enter, tainments within the reach of almost everyone.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
Who is the erring and would-be-earning Couneillcir ?
* * * Ratepayers are thankful for small mercies. A reduction of 2d, in the rates is better than the proverbial "smack in the face." * *

Two handsome legacies to the Infirmary and Dispensary are announced, the Hon. Treasurer having received an intimation that the late Miss Margaret Garven and the late Rev. Edward Dakin Garven have each bequeathed £5OO to the institution.

* * Heard outside the Academy on Monday night: " That's the Town Hall or something ; funny place isn't it '4" Such is fame ! We may add that the commentator was a stranger to Warrington, and the hour was late, very late!

We are informed that the CNservative whip was very busy on Monday and Tuesday. Conservative Town Councillors and Aldermen, with one or two notable exceptions, were afraid—yes afraid—to vote as they would have liked at the Aldermanic election. What is going to happen next? * * *

Mr. J. Keir Hardie, M.P., got ,out of his latitude, in a literal sense, the other day. He was announced to address a Labour demonstration at Famworth (Bolton) but by some mischance was taken to the wrong Farn- worth, near Widnes. The result was that at audience of 2,000 waited in vain for his appearance, and at length had to golome disappointed. * * *

George Jacob Holyoake celebrated his 88th birthday on Thursday last. We are pleased to learn that the author of The Co-operative Movement To-day " "The History of Co-operation in England," "The Rochdale Pioneers " etc., etc., is in excellent health. May he continue to teach us our duties. We cordially him "Many happy returns of the day."

* * * When is Warrington Bridge going to be widened? The Town Council does not know, though it authorised the work and let the contract Months ago. Alderman Smethurst swears he will find out who is keeping the matter back or call a public meeting. Go a head, Mr. Alderman,we will back you up. The scheme has been travestied long enough, and the artful obstructors with selfish ends in view have had too much of their own way. * * *

Councillor Stott has ideas of his own as to the people who should be disfranchised. In arguing that persons who accept poor law relief should be exempt, he said that " only criminals, idiots, and members of the House of Peers should be disfranchised "—a sally which provoked much laughter even from the staunch adherents of Church and State. Might we ask the Labour member whether it is the idiots or the criminals with whom he classes the peers ? * * *

One of the. last charges we should have thought of making against his Worship the Mayor is that of being ungallant to the fair sex. But at the Council meeting he was convicted out of his own mouth of this heinous offence. There was a discussion ob the appointment of a successor to Mr. F. Monks on the Education Com- mittee, and Alderman Pier Point suggested that a lady should be nominated, in preference to Mr. Henry Roberts. The Mayor remarked that he thought " it would not be very complimentary to Mr. Monks to put a lady in his place." Fie upon you,Mr. Mayor ! You are not complimentary to the ladies, and we are,surc Mr. Monks would'disagree with you. - * * *

Councillor Pemberton said on Tuesday that he under- stood the Musetun Curator's duties included "the stuffing and mounting of birds and animals." Some- how or other we cannot imagine Mr. Madeley endeavouring to fill out the skin of a defunct lion and give it the semblance of life. It is not believed that he does anything of the kind. Such work is sent out. Alderman Bennett waxed wroth at the suggestion and accused Councillor Pemberton of thinking the Museum it sort of "inanimate menagerie " in his " childlike ignorance." • Somebody has to stuff the birds and fishes, and we should like to know who is the borough taxidermist. * * *

Hardly a day passes without our being stopped by men who are ' hard up,' asking alms like poor slaves in past days. Would that we had a bottomless purse that we might help all the needy until such times that they could get work, and food for themselves and their little ones. The pity of it. The shame, too, that the sympathetic givers should be made fools of by those who would rather drink than work. We have helped individuals in the morning coming to business and have found the cringing hypocrites lying drunk in the gutter before evening. A plausible tale can be told by a scamp as well as by an honest man. It should not stop us from helping, however, but it should teach us to be more careful in our methods.

" The'Dawn" ie getting strong in its opinions. In an article on " Local Architecture " in this month's issue, our local buildings are held up to scorn and ! ridicule. We do not agree with all that the writer says, but with much we are in sympathy. " When . we sit down to build, we do not ask, will such and ' Such an edifice be an ornament to the town and a credit to the town and neighbourhood ?'—' a thing of • beauty and a joy for ever ?'—but Will it last my time and bring me in so much per cent., and turn each miserable inch of earth into an income ?'" We are such mercenary beings—thanks to our social and com- petitive systems—that we are always " on the make." God and the human race disappear when we count our coins. Humanity is then an idle dream.
PAGE

What has become of the resuscitated Y.A.C.A.? We were hoping that the young men of Wariington would have combined to form a strong Society. The fault of the old Association lay in its management. What is needed is an Institute, as Dr. Diggle stated at Carlisle the other evening in connection with the diamond jubilee of Y.M.C.A.'s, which can be "made more use of as a training ground for civic, municipal, and possibly for national life." Dr. Diggle believed that there was "nothing terrific about smoking, and if young men could not smoke at the Y.M.C:A. they would go to some place where they could." A "home from home" for namby-pamby, goody-goody individual's, and a stronghold for evangelical hot-house plants, is not likely to be successful, now-a-days. .Let there be some " robustness " about the affair and we shall welcome it. *

" Afy Lords and Gentlemen "!—The building up of a great party occupies the time and attention of these "My Lords and Gentlemen " and it is unfortunate that the inclinations of men differ so much that party weal should be made public woe. It were a pity that the Houses' of Parliament should be divided, and that men should sacrifice their consciences and con- victions rather than give their support to a bill which happens to be introduced by their political antagonists. But public opinion is now becoming so educated— thanks to peisons who hitherto have not aspired to political fame—that social questions will have to be considered, and seriously too, by those who have received the votes of the majority in their respective constituencies. If they fail to put into practice the promises they made with such fluency of speech and with tears in their voice the mystic letters will no longer be appended to their already long and fashion- able names. And what will they do then, poor things? * * *

, It is remarkable what a lot of pain and inconveni- ence footballers will undergo in their love for the game. T. Hockenhall,Warridgton's County half-back, has sustained a fractured collar-bone three times in his comparatively short career. The misfortune has happened twice this season. On Saturday he rejoined the team after two months absence, and on Monday evening in a match at Widnes he vas again injured in just the Same way. Either the popular half-back's collar-bone is especially brittle or else he is the accursed of Dame Fortune. Non-athletic readers will probably say " football is a brutal game," but simple fractures are sustained very easily and are not often an indication of roughness. Another Warrington man, Hughes of Widnes, has had a leg broken this season; and is now playing as wel,l as ever; while Preston, a Warrington forward, was only out of the game for a few weeks with a broken wrist-bone. When you get thirty men per match strenuously engaged there are , bound to be accidents. They will happen in the best regulated games, and one feels a certain amount of adMiration for the plucky fellows who endure the I buffets of misfortune so philosophically in their love of sport.

The" George " Licence. At a meeting of the Compensation Authority for the Borough, which consists of the whole Bench of magistrates, the report of the Licensing Justices with regard to the "George "Hotel licence was adopted It will be remembered that at the recent Licensing Sessions it was decided to renew the licence provision- ally, pending a consideration of the compensation question. By adopting the report the Compensation Authority agreed to compensation being given, and all that now remains to be done is to assess the amount. public meeting of the justices will be held in due c rse to arrange this matter.

• " PREMIER CYCLES at 7 guineas startling value.— J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 53, Bridge st., Warrington.— Advt. Gas Explosion at the Town Hall. Mt. Powis, the caretaker of the Town Hall and his wife were wakened early on Sunday morning ,by the sound of an explosion. 'Mr..Powis at once arose and made an inspection bf the buildhig and found the rafters near the tea room on the ground floor were in flames. Mr. Powis at once extinguished the flames. The force of the explosion was so great that it blew the plaster off the rafters in the passage a few yards away, and also blew out a large square of glass nem% the door which leads into the building.. The stones II the floor just over the scene of the explosion were also dislodged. The explosion is said to be (hie to he fusing of an electric wire which melted the adjoin- g gas pipe. •

The " Y's " at Work. The first business meeting of the "Y" Branch of the British Women's Temperance Association was held in the Church Parlour at Bold-street on Monday and proved a very successful gathering. The President, Miss Dutton, took the chair, and the following officers were elected:—Miss Gornall, treasurer ; Miss M. Dodds, secretary ; Miss Walker, recording secretary; Committee, Miss Watson, Miss Bindloss, Miss Jackson, Miss A. Langdon, Miss Atkinson, Mrs. Noble, Mrs., Stowe, Mrs. Milne, Miss Beswick, Miss Fieldhouse. Miss Dutton gave a abort address on the aims and character of the association and made several useful suggestions. It was decided that the next meeting should be held on Thursday afternoon Ma Y 4th, the business of which vill be to arrange for an A.B.C. (Aprons, _Buns and Cakes) Sale to be • held early in June to provide working expenses..

There was a good attendance in the Cairo-street schools on Wednesday evening,at a Shakespearean and humorous recital, given under the auspices of the Warrington Independent Labour Party. The elocutionist was Mr. Edmund Spencer, who greatly pleased the audience by his selections from "Hamlet," "Henry VIII.," and "School for Scandal." Enjoyable selec- tions *ere also given by Mrs. Spencer and the tEolian Glee Party.

div.head: Good News for Foundry Workmen.
div.p: Good News for Foundry Workmen.

Notwithstanding extensive foreign competition, the Vulcan Foundry, Limited, of Newton-le-Willows, on Saturday morning received information that they have secured the contract•for the building of thirty standard goods engines and tenders. During the past fort- night the same firm have also received orders- for fifteen heavy goods engines and tenders for the Buenos Ayres Great Southern Railway and five tank and shunting engines for the Buenos Ayres and Rosario Railway. The trade in the district will in consequence receive a large and welcome fillip, and these orders alone will keep the firm's employees - working full time during the whole of this year. ,
FOR Smart up-to-date COSTUMES, try PATTISON AND PERKINS, 17, SANKEY STREET.—Advt.

div.head: National Union of Teachers.
div.p: The National Union of Teachers.

• The thirty-sixth annual Conference of the National Union of Teachers is to be held in Llandudno during Easter week. The gatherings will commence on April 20th; but the Conference proper will open at 11 a.m. on Monday, April 24th, and close on the following Thursday. The chair will be taken by Mr. Tom John, the president-elect, of Thepvynpia Schools, Rhondda, from whom a presidential address, dealing powerfully with current questions of educational interestSmhy be expected. An important programme of motions on educational subjects will be discussed. It is antici- pated that over 2,000 teachers will be present, as the appointed representatives of the 470 branches of the Union. The Conference Will also receive deputations of teachers from Scotland, Ireland, Belgium and France, and a deputation from the Co-operative Union will also attend the Conference.—The Warrington delegates are Mrs. StanS'field, Miss Brookes, and Messrs. Dewhurst, C4nn, Cawthorne, Jeffrey, Upson, Wallington, Stanstield, and Wright.

div.head: Breakfastless School Children.
div.p: Breakfastless School Children.

Free breakfasts of dry bread and cocoa have again been provided this week at the Ragged school each morning from 745 to 90. Forty-four were present on Monday, 50 on Tuesday, GO on Wednesday, 71 on Thursday. About 10 per cent of the whole have been nearly every morning, both last week and this. Forty- one additional children came this week for the first time. Five hundred and tWenty-one breakfasts have been given altogether up to Thursday morning to 150 different children. The Executive Conimittee thank- fully acknowledge ,donationS of one ton of coal from Messrs. Richardson, and 53,6.6 d, from the Warrington Trades and Labour Council (per Councillor Stott). The ss. acknowledged last week as from the Warring- ton Independent Labour Party was an error, as the donation was from the Warrington Labour Representa- tion Committee. Unless there is a far more liberal response to the appeal of the Mission for assistance, the breakfasts will have t-) be discontinued. The Ragged School authorities submit that they have proved the sad fact that many children are sent to school to be educated and to the tzmulasium to receive physical training without having had any breakfast whatever ; whilst a large number never get half ough. The remedy lies wtli.other authorities. Ass for Cusxmosiat's HIGII-CLA.Eb MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Sale of Work at Latchford.

A sale of work was opened on Thursday in the , Knutsford-road Primitive Methodist Mission, with the object of liquidating the debt on the Mission arising from re-decoration. Mr. C. E. Parker had been announced to preside but wrote, enclosing a cheque for £5, and expressing his inability to attend. Mr. J. Whitley presided over a good attendance and in asking Mrs. J. Dodds to open the sale, remarked that every Christian or philanthropic work which had for its object the uplifting of the masses received valuable help from Mr.and Mrs.Dodds. (Hear, hear.) They had done a great deal on behalf of churches in the neighbourhood and were widely known and respected for their good ' work. He hoped that the Church would prosper more ' and more as time went on. (Applause.) • Mrs. Dodds who was accorded a hearty reception, expressed her pleasure at being present. She said she must con- gratulate them upon the display of goods for sale, and wished them in the highest and best sense every success in their work. (Applause.).- She had pleasure in declaring the sale open. —Mrs. Dodds was heartily thanked for her services and the sales for the clay commenced. The stalls, which contained a variety of articles were in charge of the following ladies : Mesdames Canning, Harding and Barber (Knutsford-road ladies' stall), Dalton, Podinore, Atkinson (Leigh-street stall), Cotterill and Matthews (children's stall), Stowe and Brooks (Christian Endeavour stall) and Ciriffith, Spruce, Sparks, Barber and Leather (refreshment stall).
