div.head: NEW ALDERMAN.
div.p: THE NEW ALDERMAN.
BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCH.

' The elevation of Councillor David Tinnion to an aldermanic seat is the fitting reward of useful and diligent public service. A native of Maryport,Cumber- land,Aldennan Tinnion came to Warrington as a youth in 1878 to take charge of the commercial department at the works of Messrs. Henry Kenyon and Co., spelter manufacturers. He has thrown himself into the business with enery and aptitude until he is now the proprietor of the works. As an enthusiastic member of the Liberal party, Alderman Tinnion has taken an active interest in politics ever since the election of 1885 when the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., defeated Mr. Wm. Crosfield by 776 votes. He has rendered assistance during election campaigns in every ward in the town, but of course his interests have been more particularly centred in St. Austin's Ward. He has held the offices of chairman and deputy chairman of the Ward Com- mittee for fifteen years. In the work of the Liberal Association and Club he has long played a prominent and valued part, and for four ye ire he has presided , over the Executive Committee of the Association. He lhas acted as Chairman of the Liberal Club for about twelve years, and the development of the social side of , politics has received every encouragement and help from him. His career as a member of the Town Council began in 1895 when he contested St. Austin's I ! Ward against Mr. William Gill. The question before the electors was the proposal to establish a cattle !market on the site of the present Police I Station and the light was entered into with considerable vigour, Mr. Tinnion achieving I the victory. When he had been a member ' of the Council for twelve months the extension of the Borough necessitated the retirement of the three repre- sentatives of the ward, and the ensuing election resulted in the return of three Lib ends—Mt. Tinnion, Mr. T. Burton, and the late Mr. John Crosfield. As Mr. Tinnion obtained the Largest majority he held a seat in the Council for three years without a break. Since then he has fought two elec- tions and has been victorious on each occasion. He has devoted a great deal of time to committee work and is at present chairman of the Paving and Sewerage and Gymnasium Committees. I Alderman Tinnion is one of the oldest, if not the ! oldest member of the Warrington Football Club, and , at one time played as a forward. For twenty years he has been connected with the Warrington Crioket Club, I and has discharged the duties of hon. auditor for twelve years. . . . .

A Wesleyan in religion, Alderman Tinnion has long been identified with Bewsey-road Church. Prior to the passing' of the Education Act he was a manager of Silver-street and Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Day , Schools, and since the new authority came into exist- ence he has acted as a representative manager of People's College. His numerous friends will heartily cougratulatehim upon the hguour which the Council have seen fit to confer upon him, and that he has many years of public service before him will, we are sure, be their unani- mous wish. With to-day's issue of the " Examiner " we present our readers with a supplement ccutaining a portrait of Alderman Tinnion.

div.head: LOCAL EDUCATION
div.p: LOCAL EDUCATION
From the Workingman's Standpoint. THE HEADMISTRESS OF HOLY TRINItY
SCHOOLS.

At a meeting of the Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday evening, Mr. E. Plinston presented au interest- ing report on the two years' work of the Education Committee on which authority he represents the Council. To his mind, he said, it nes as yet too early to ex,nect a full return fcr the increased expenditure upon Education in Warrington. The education of the rising generation was the most important question before the country, for the future of the nation depended on a thorough, and complete elementary and secondary education being given to all children, irresp3c- Live of rank or station. The only occasion upon which the Education Committee had come into conflict with th 3 Town Council was /upon the question of the annual increment of the teachers' salaries. The Council appeared to hese lost sight of the fact that the proper time to raise objections was when the scale of salaries adopted by the authority was submitted to them. When that fact was pointed out it was at once seen that the friction might have been avoided. As evidence of the fact that

NO RELIGIOLV ANIMUS had appeared in the working of the committee he might say that he was unanimously selected as a repre- sentative manager of a Roman Catholic school, and since then a Roman Catholic had been appointed to a similar position in respect of a Nonconformist school. That, in his opinion, was just as things ought to be. The most important work which had devolved upon him had been in nouns .:tiou with the School Attendance Committe3. Daring the past twelve months he had attended all the meetings of the authority with the exception of one,in addition to thirty-six weokly rota me3tings for school attend ince p mpos.s. He wanted it to be understood that while he was fully aware that regular attendance was the only means by which a thorough education conld be fecsived and that the grants were now paid on the attendance instead of on results, he felt bound to support the granting of exemptions to the children of people whose exceedingly poor circumstances made the matter of obtaining their living more important even than education. Where such conditions did not arise he would at all times agree with the enforcing of attnnd- ance, except in cases of sickness. On mmy occasions children wore absent from school benuse through poverty they were usable to obtain sufficient clothing and food. In his view it was absolutely essential to the proper management of school attendance that the committee which had to deal with

_ THE ENFORCEMENT Ole ATTENDANCE should also be able not only to authorize the giving of relief to deserving cases, but hive thepower to actually grant the relief. Mr. Plinstou alluded to the request of prominent medical practitioners that the Education Committee should support a petition with the object of making the teaching of hygiene and temperance com- pulsory in the day schools. He did not think the committee acted wisely in deciding not to take action in the matter because they believed the present volun- tary instruction was more effective. In view of the importance of the question of the effects of alcohol I it would have been better had the committee insisted that teachers should be thoroughly and effici- ently instructed on the matter, so as to be able to point out to the scholars the detrimental influence of alcohol upon the human system. During the past few weeks a question of importance to one of the head teachers had been brought before the public—he referred to the attempt that was made to deprive the

div.head: HEADNIISTRRSS OP HOLY TRINITY SCHOOL
div.p: HEADNIISTRRSS OP HOLY TRINITY SCHOOL

of the annual increment to whickshe was entitled accord- ing to the scale. Vague charges were made against the teacher, but unfortunately no opportunity was given her ofing appear before the committee,although she was quite willing to do so, before the penalty was indicted. He maintained that before any person was punished the (fence alleged should be absolutely proved. The ques- tion was not yet settled, but it was his intention to see that full and ample justice was done in that case. Mr. , Plinstoa alluded to the result of the recent KING'S SCHOLARSHIP EXAMINATION. They were told by the CIIi.IRMAN of the School Management Committee that there was nothing to be alarmed about. While looking upon the Rev. Morley Stevenson as an authority on such questions, he (Mr. Plinston) was of opinion that seeing that batter facilities were now given for the instruction of pupil teachers and that the expenditure on that depsrtment was far in advance of the suns spent under ths old system, the results ought to have been far more satis- factory. It was to be hoped that if anyone was at , fault, an improvement would take place. Mr. Plinston proceeded to argue that it was a mistake to dispense with MN-CERTIFICATED TEACHERS

who had served the schools well in the past and who through no fault of their own, but probably owing to financial inability, had been unable to thoroughly qualify themselves. Many had already been forced to leave Warrington and obtain similar places elsewhere, as the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils and other authorities engaged such teachers. Mr. Plinston alluded to the great necessity for dealing with the over. 1 crowding question, pointing out that until more adequate I accommodation was provided completely satisfactory I 1 results could not be obtained. He also briefly touched upon the recent address of Mr. S. W. Jeffrey (president of the Teachers' Association) who replied to the argu- ment of Mr. Walker as to the danger of setting too high an ideal in educational matters. He (Mr. Plinston) partially agreed with Mr. Walker, because while he admitted that the fullest education should be given, he thought the possibilities of each child should be taken into consideration. In the cases where children were destined to follow their parents in the ordinary labour- ing classes too much education might be possible, but in most cases a thorough elementary and secondary education should be placed within the reach of all. He would,however,lik e to see the day when such a secondary education would be given as wAtild prepare the children to take their places in different trades and qualify them for higher positions than they would otherwise have been able to obtain. Mr. Plinston made a short refer- ehce to the retirement of Mr. F. Monks from the chairmanship of the committee. Mr. Monks was,

in his (the speaker's) opinion one of the leading educa- tionists, and although they might differ from him on many questions, they must admit that from his point of view he always worked with the full intention of placing the educational life of Warrington in the forefront. It would 133 difficult to find a successor who would be able to place such valuable services at the disposal of the committee. In conclusion Mr. Plinston said his work on the Education Committee would always be directed to the one object of placing a thorough and practical education within the reach of all. (Applause). Au interesting discnssion followed, after which . .

Mr.Jot.r.n Moved a vote of thank Sto Mr. Plinston,re- , marking that they could not have had a more able report. The Council ought to keep its eye on the educational expenditure, particularly in the payment for sites. The Committee ought not to pay such an exorbitant price as was given forland at Latchford when surrounding land might have been obtained for considerably less. He was sure the Council would agree with Mr. Plinston in his attitude with regard to uncertiflcated teachers. Councilor SroTT intimated that he wrote to Mr. Plinston thanking him, on behalf of the Council. for his action in regard to the head mistress of Holy Trinity schools. Several membere,supported the vote of thanks which was heartily accorded. PLINSTON in reply alluded to the heavy price paid for lend at Latchford and said the Town Council was told by the Mayor that the Government Inspector would not approve of any other site. The question of uncertift- cated teachers would have to be fought and he believed it would be a severe battle.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
(By " Oyalist.",

" Warrington's winning way," as " Philistine " describes it, has been proved again at the expense of Salford and Widnes, and the supporters of the Club are hopeful that it will be maintained for just two more cup-ties. To-day we have the semi-finals on hand,with Warrington once more particiPating.Their opponents are , the doughtiest team in the League so that Warrington could not have a task better calculated to extend their capabilities to the fall. Bradford are old opponents, and to-day's meeting will be the seventh between the two teams in two seasons. A year ago the semi-finals brought Warrington and Bradford together at Broughton, a drawn game being the result. The re- play at Huddersfield was signalised by a great War_ I rington triuuiph. Doubtless the 'Bradford men are itching for their revenge and will leave nothing untried in their endeavour to obtain it to-day. 1

There is as much confidence in Warrington as ever there was, and the "winning way " of late has stamped the team with the hall-mark of excellence. They are playing better now than at any time during the season and granted a continuance of the good-for. tine which has certainly attended them of late they should achieve tie height of their ambition and win the cup. A year ago there was a lamentable want of a continuance of form in the final and Warrington's hopes were blighted. They may, of course, not reach the final this time, but I am nelying on the "winning way "to pull them through.

--- A big feature in Warrington's recent steccesses has been their good fortune in scoring first. 'Every match recently, including all cup-ties, they have notched the first point, and how valuable an asset this is, only the players can tell. Nothing succeeds like success, and if Warrington are the first to score to-day I shall be confident in their ultimate victory.

Salford made their annual visit to Wilderspool on Saturday, and contrary to their epectations they did not find Warrington willing victims. Last year Warrington were saving themselves for the cup and gave the Reds a virtual walk-over. Apparently they were no better off for the humiliation of an accepted defeat, and on Saturday they altered their tactics. True, there was little of the do or die about the match, but Warrington always seemed the more capable side and probably had more in hand than a five points to nil victory would suggest. At the outset, the combination of the backs was brilliant in the extreme and three tries ought to have been 'registered. Carelessness, how- ever, spoiled the efforts. Once Fish overran Isher- wood when the centre had made a perfect opening, and such a fault by an accomplished player like Fish is unpardonable. No wonder " Danny " as annoyed and said no. At half-time Warrington were a goal to the good. In the second half they played very slackly, and Salford quite held their own until near the close. Then the homesters asserted themselves and vigorous attack resulted in Davies obtaining a good try. The match was memorable for two things. One was the return of Hockenhall after two months' absence through injury. The popular half-back played a fair game, but was not in his, best form by any means, and Davies showed the more cleverness. ;The second event was one of a sad description. Lambert, the promising young Salford full- back stumbled in running for the ball and fractured his knee-cap —oae of the worst mishaps which could ' befall an athlete. It was' a remarkable accident for there was not a man within yards of him, and he fell ' quite easily. The medical opinion is that a sudden contraction of the muscles split the knee-cap, which was not due to the fall. Anyhow it was a most unfortunate affair, anal it terminates Lambert's career as a footballer. At pr 'eat he is an inmate of the Warrington Infirmary,

On Monday, Warrington paid Widnes a return visit, and there was a Lard fight for points. Both teams were triers and there was nothing' of the kid- glove character about the play. Warrington main- tained their form and .won by the big margin of 18 points to 6 points. There was hardly this difference between the teams, but the way Warrington snapped up chances soon left the home lot in the rear. Speedy following up by both forwards and backs Had a lot to do With the scoring, for some of the home defenders were very unsteady when pressed. Isherwood, Kenyon, and Hallam played grandly, the right-winger showing an amount of dash and pace which astonished the natives. He was unlucky in not having a try to his credit. Fish scored one of his own special type of tries by intercepting ! a Widnes pass and generally showed good form. In fact the team was too good altogether for Widnes, though the latter were full of energy and determina- tion.

The sweets of victory were, however, spoiled by the bitter of adversity. liockenhall's ill-luck sticks to him and near the close of the 'game he sustained another fracture of the left-collar-bone. The incident was. exactly simile to the one at Runcorn in February. ockenhall broke away cleverly and parted with the ball, only to be foully charged over and injured_ Could anyone be more unfortunate? The accident puts the County man out of the running for cup-tie honours, if there are any, and deprives the club of a valuable man ' They will be compelled to do without Hockenhall for 'the rest of the season, and everything depends now on Brooks and Davies.

Prior to Saturday the League championship seemed a safe thing for Oldham, but they received a rude rebuff at the hands of Broughton Rangers. Seventeen points to nil fairly staggered other people besides the Oldhtm men, who appeared either stale or " down- hearted !' by cup-tie failure. Both the Rangers and Bradford are row once more in the running. War- rington tie NVith Leeds for fourth place.

After all Warrington have an outside chance of retainivg possession of the South-West Lancashire Cup. The chances are as follows : Warrington will probably beat St. Helens here on Good Friday and thus total 15 points. If Leigh lose at Widnes on Saturday and win at Wigan on Good Friday Warrington go to the head of affairs. Should Leigh win at Widnes they will be tied to win at Wigan in order to secure the trophy. A draw at Wigan would make the three clubs equal. The odds are certainly on Wigan for the Cup, however, as they have only to beat Leigh to finish up a point ahead of everybody.

The "A" team made no mistake at Salford and won by eight points to nil,Brooks and Jordan scoring clever tries. Warrington's combination was much too good for the Reds. Theye has been no complete record of the Combination table published of late, but I wilt endeavour to make the respective positions of War - rin,gton and Wigan clear next week.

div.head: SEMI-FINAL TEAMS.
div.p: THE SEMI-FINAL TEAMS.

The Warrington team for the semi-final was selected on Wednesday evening, :Lid is exactly the same as against Wigan, viz.: Hallam, full back; Fish, Isher- wood, Dickenson and Kenyon, three-quarters; D. Davies and Brooks, half-backs; 'Preston, Boardman, Shugars, Thomas, Naylor, Jolley, Belton and Swift, forwards.- The men have been training during the week, and though several feel the effects of the Widnes encounter and have not been working continuously since, they are all expected to be fit to-dly. Of their confidence there is no question. Nearly every titan has' " backed" Warrington.

There will be three special trains from Warrington to Rochdale to-day, fare 2s. 6d. return. The London. and North-Western are running through trains at 1-10 and 1-55. I should advise as many as can to, travel by the earlier of the two trains. The Cheshire Lines Company have a special at 1-5 due Rochdale at 2-25, and in addition are offering excursion bookineg to Manchester by.trains leaving at 12-50, 1-35 and 1-55, with' connections • from Victoria Station, Man- chester. The team will travel, via Manchester, by the 1-35 train. •

A NOTE FROM BRADFORD. Wiring yesterday (Friday) my Bradford correspond- ent says the Bradford team will be: Gunn, full back ; Connell, Mosby, Eagers, and Dunhavin, threequarters; Marsden and Surman, half-backs; Laidlavr, Turner, Francis, Feather, Greenwood, Sharratt, Thresh, Smales, Barker, Rees, and Westmorland (forwards selected from.) It was not expected Dechan would be able to turn out. There was also some doubt respecting the 'con- dition of Marsden, but he is now declared to be in excellent trim. The other members of the team are in capital form, though under no special training.
The following officials have been . appointed for the semi-final ties:—

Bradford v. Warrington at Rochdale. Referee, Mr. A. Smith (Halifax) ; touch judges, Messrs. W. ) Lancaster (Rochdale) and R. H. Moore (Oldham). Broughton Rangers v. Hull Kingston Rovers, at Wakefield. Referee, Mr. W. McCutcheon (Oldham); touch judges, Messrs. F. Asquith (Wakefield), alla P. W. Tattersall (Normanton).

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

The pretty C'aeshite village of Lower Peover was the destination of the Warrington Cycling Club on Saturday and seventeen members had a most enjoyable outing. The weather was flue, but there was a keenness in the atmosphere, while the roads were in excellent condition A capital tea was provided at the Warren do Ta.bley Arms by Host Bell and afterwards:a couple of hours were spent in conviviality. The homeward journey was acooinplised in good time, and the visit was voted a complete success. To-day the club journey to Helaby.

I Wheolers are looking forw.trd with pleasure to the Easter Holidays and as they are later than nsaal this years, the hopes for fine weather era more confluent. The usual tours have been arranged end the Warrington Club will spend the week-end in North Wales. The cycling season really begins in earnest at Easter, and given genial climatic conditions the various country and seaside resorts will have their full quota of visitors.

Just before Easter is the time when the ardent cyclist either treats himself to a new cycle or furnishes up his old one. Tyres are always an important consideration, and I may perhaps be permitted to give some advice based on a fairly lengthy experience. Just now the tyre makers generally seem to be producing roadster tyres with an eye to appearance and lightness rather I than durability. Most of the tyres we have examined and tried are too thin in the tread aver to be good for more than a season's riding. Competition and the cutting of prices have a lot to do with this, but there is no reason why th 3 cyclist should suffer if he is cautious. Quite the best tyre I have tried is the Palmer, which has more " body" in the tread than any r have seen for a long time. A pair in use at present seem to defy punctures and obviate pumping, except at very rare intervals, while they are exceptionally comfortable on setts and rough surfaces. A speciality of Palmer tyres is the inner fabric, which is not woven, but composed of parallel threads embedded in the best auality of rubber. There is no friction as between the threads of the woven fabric. and the wearing/qualities of the tyre are thus enhanced

Bowling. Next Saturday will witness the opOning of the majority of the bowling greens in Warrington and local enthusiasts are high in their expectations of a, successful seahon. The greens are, with probably one exception, all in excellent condition and some close games should result during the season.

On Thursday night the committee of the Warrington and District Bowling League held a meeting at the , Cemetery hotel, at which it was found necessary to alter several of the fixtures. The match between the Bull's Head and the Penketh Park teams on the gteen of the first Darned club will be played on June 3rd instead of on June 24th, while the Cemetery team will visit. Penketh Park on August 19th instead of June 3rd. As was the case last year, greens w ill be open to practice by players in visiting teams from one o'clock until two o'clock. As was announced last week, the first of a series of mains open to the members of the League will be held on the Cemetery Green on May 15th. Entries will close at 7 o'clock on the day previous.

One of the most important items under discussion was the gift made by Mr. England of .£5 for a cham- pionship prize to be competed for by Warrington bowlers. Mr. England suggested that the main should be opened to all bowlers resident within three miles of the town, but such a suggestion was somewhat imprac- ticable on account of the large number of players resi- dent within that radius who might enter the competition This was pointed out to Mr. England who decided to leave the matter in the hands of the Warrington and District Bowling League. After considerable discussion the League decided to suggest that the prize should be competed by two players from each club connected , with the League with the highest aggregate score in league matches, the main, subject 1.0 the consent of the Corporation, to be decided on the Victoria Park Green.

Their decision will hardly I think, meet Mr. England's wishes. The original intention was that the competi- tion should be open to all Warrington players and the suggestion of the League will considerably restrict the number able to take part. It must be admitted that some of the finest trundlers of the town are connected with the League but there is considerable doubt as to whether their members include the cream of local bowlers, I would suggest that players of undoubted ability connected with any club should be allowed to compete, the players to be selected by and to represent the club with which they are connected. The winner under such conditions would more fully deserve the title of champion than thc winner on the line suggested by the League.

Mr. E. England also offered to snbscribe Zi is. a year for the provision of an annual prize. The offer is an excellent one and one which ought to be accepted pro- vided of course that other gentlemen will make a equally generous offer.

div.head: Cricket.
div.p: Cricket.

While football cuo ties are monopolising public attention, cricket has to take a back seat. The War- rington Cricket Club should have opened their season to-day with a match against representatives of teams of Warring and District, but owing to the enormous amount of interest which is being taken in the semi- final at Rochdale, the fixture has fallen through. The season will therefore open on Saturday next when War- rington will journey to Bolton. The eleven is practically the same as last year's with the exception that Lynes, the professional, who has gone to Bacup, will be succeeded by Mason. of Bootle, who formerly played for Notts. A successful season is anticipated.

Why should not Warrington have a Junior Cricket League? There is plenty of junior talent and enthusiasm in the town, and such an organization would do a great deal to increase interest in the sport. There seems to be no reason why the representatives of the various clubs shoula not arrange a meeting which would result in the formation of a strongleague.

At noon on Thursday a man under the influence or drink deliberately kicked in two large plate glass win- dows at a furnishing establishment in London road, Manchester, and he was only just prevented from breaking a third.

div.head: BUTTONS AND BUCKLES.
div.p: BUTTONS AND BUCKLES.

Antique silver buttons are just now tremendously popular. Button-trimmings are a rage at he present moment, says a (i/obe writer, and old silver, or copies, are seen to much advantage on the taffetas and voile pictures-gowus that obtain. A pretty button in green enamel has a wreath of little silver Cupids in relief all round it: another, in silver, with a beaded edge, has a border of tiny rose-sprays, while one larger spray adorns the centre. Circles of alternate diamonds and emeralds or ruldcs are very effective,i and a pretty marquise. shaped button is n gold edged with pearls. Little miniatures set in oxydised filigree Nvork are again fashionable crystal buttons are much worn, and mother-o'-pearl, particularly smoked to a half- dark shade. Enamel buttons are always in favour, since they may be had to match any gown. In buckles there is an enormous variety. A pretty specimen is in dull, rough silver with a bright beading, dotted with tiny gems of subdued tints done in enamel. From Japan comes a grey metal buckle shaded like a river with a breeze on it. Up one side are one or two slender silver rushes, and a translucent white water-lily is indicated at their feet. Perfectly plain buckles and slides of polished gold are worn a good deal. Their simplicity is a welcome change after the reign of senseless intricacy.

div.head: SMART COSTIIMZ.
div.p: A SMART COSTIIMZ.

Silks of all kinds are going to be much warn during the coming season. The smart costume shewn in the sketch was composed of a very small black-and-white check silk. The bodice, or coat, is made over a tight-fitting foundation of black taffetas, which comes to a deep point at the front, and is ornamented with dull gold buttons. The small frills of checked silk are only ',lightly gathered on to the foundation. At the neck there

is a scroll-shaped collar of black taffetas, finished with buttons. The sleevea are full at the shoulder, and are gathered into a tight band at the elbow, and further trimmed with knife-pleated frills of taffetas. The skirt is gathered full into the waistband, and trimmed below the knees with Pleated frills of taffetas to match the sleeves. A smart little hat of geranium-coloured straw, trimmed with geraniums and leaves, adds a touch of colour to the costume.

div.head: MILLINERY Nor.
div.p: MILLINERY Nor.

A novel ornament seen recently .on a large blacks picture hat of Parisian origin is a medallion worked in the old-fashioned beadwork which has been so largely exploited of lath in the form of bags and belts. A feather which is being used a good deal both on nart and simple millinery is a cross between a wing and a quill, having a goose-quill stem with a wing of very soft white plumage on either side. A toque of closely-massed china-blue forget-me-nots with the brim turned sharply up at one side has one of these soft white plumes laid across the side. The effect is quite good, despite the almost universal rule that flowers and feathers, like near relations, are best apart.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

FILLETS Or TURBOT OR HALIBUT A LA GENDIENNE. —Three pounds of fish, 4oz. of Patna rice, loz. of butter, two eggs, a pint of breadcrumbs, a dessert- spoonful of curry powder, one pint of milk, two bard-boiled eggs. Cut the fish from the bone, remove the skin carefully, and cut the fish into neat slices; place them in a dish, season with pepper and Alt, and pour over sufficient milk to cover. Prepare a stock from the bones by boiling them in seasoned water for half-an-hour, then strain. Cook 40z. of lice in boiling salted water for a quarter of an hour; when done, mix with a piece of butter and about a dessertspoonful of curry powder. Drain r.nd wipe the fillets, cover with egg . and bread- crumbs. fry them in deer) fat. and dram on naner before the tire. Fill a buttered i noraer-mouict with the rice and turn out on a hot dish; place the flied fish in the centre arid cover the border of rice with slices of hard-boiled egg. Send to table with a nice white sauce.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A COSTLY POSTCARD CRAZE.

At the Wa;ritc;;PO'lTC-eb-OUi:t -o-i-i--SlOnday George Stubbs, Northwich, was charged with sending postcards of a gross and offensive nature to Miss Hallwood, daughter of Mr. Hallwood, NVilderspool-road. Stubbs failed to appear in answer to a summons which was issued against him and he was on Saturday arrested on warrant.—He pleaded guilty.—Mr. Browne said that some three years ago Miss Hallwood was introduced to Stubbs and had since never seen or spoken to him. Shortly before Christmas he commenced to send her postcards, and often walked to Warrington to see Miss Hallwood, though he never succeeded in his object. The postcards were of a most offensive character. Prisoner had regarded the prosecution as a joke on the part of his brother, who was a clerk in the employment of a respectable firm of solicitors in Northwich. If prisoner would undertake not to continue his conduct he was prepared to withdraw the charge 07 payment of costs. Prisoner gave the required undertaking and was ordered by the magistrates to pay the costs—£l Including the advocates' fee.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

CROWNING THE TEMBERANCE QUEEN.—On Monday evening, the cantata "Crowning the Temperance Queen" was given by the members of Hill Chile and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope in the Providence school- room, a pretty spectacle being presented. The Rev. J. S. Hughes presided over a large attendance, and was supported by the Rev. G. H. Carnson. The children in the cantata showed they had been very carefully trained the piece being given without a single hitch, and in an excellent manner. The following items were given as interludes : "The call to the flowers," by Miss May Isherwood and a number of little girls who represented various flowers ; Miss L. Snelley contributed " The " Japanese love song" Miss Lena Duckworth 'The pigtail and the fan "and "The swallows ;" Misses E. and L. Pooley a couple of duets (violin and piano) ; whilst National Dances were much appreciated. Prizes were awarded to the following members for good attendance :—Active service and good behaviour, to May Isherwood, Arthur Whit- field, Emma Hamblett, Elsie Whitfield, Edith Hamblett Joseph Whitfield, and Arthur Hughes ; whilst a number of members also received a certificate of merit for the same object. A prize was presented to Edith Coles for selling the largest number of tickets. The list of characters was as follows :—Retiring Queen, Jessie Ellison ; Queen-elect, Eunice Downs ; first herald, T. Richmond ; second herald, S. Jonds ; doorkeeper, A. Whitfield ; page, T. Pearse ; Faith, E. Harublett ; Hope, M. Vern= ; Love, E. Coles ; Mercy, C. T, Caine ; Thrift, M. Earle ; Industry, E. Hamblett ; Peace, M. Begg ; trainbearers, G. Chile, E. Bailey, M. Cain, J. Adams, guards, J. Whitfield, A. Hughes, \V. Andrews, H. Jones, .1. Yould, and C. Bailey; Cruelty, S. Bate ; Sorrow, E. Gamble.—On the proposition of Mr. G. Whitfield (the secretary) a hearty vote of thanks was accorded all who had taken part in the entertainment, including Mrs. Davenport and Miss Wilson (trainers), Mr. E. T. Ellison (conductor), Mrs. Hughes and Miss Lomas (accompanists), and Mr. E. Wallington (head- master of the People's College) for use of costumes. ALLEGED NEOLF.CT OF CHILDREN*—At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday Thomas Bushel,lleath-street, Stockton Heath,' was charged with neglecting his five children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary snflering and injury to health.—Mr. Browne, solicitor, who appeared on behalf of the N.S.P.O C., said that the defendant was apprehended on a warrant for the neglect and illtreatruent of his children. Unfortunately, he only came out of prison on Thursday or Friday last. having been committed for debt. Drink was the whole cause of the trouble, but the imprisonment seemed to have made another man of him, and his wife said she would now give him another chance. He was brought ma at the Warrington Occasional Court on Saturday, when he undertook to sign the pledge. He had done that and assured him (Mr. Browne) that he would in f,pture endeavour to do his best for his wife and family. As he thought the defendant would now turn over a new leaf, he would suggest an adjournment of the case for three months.—The Chairman said the Bench would be pleased to agree to that course, as they were only too glad to see that end to the proceedings The N.S.P.C.C. they knew desired to secure the welfare of the children, and he hoped the wife and children would benefit by the soclety't actions in this case.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The King and Queen.—Their Majesties' holiday cruise has been continued under more favourable conditions than marked its commencement, when the Queen and Royal (party experienced so much bad weather. For many years the Queen has made a point of spending her father's birthday in Denmark, but though King Christian , has turned eighty-seven' he is younger than his years, and in such good health that her Majesty decided to continue her stay by the sunny shores of the Mediteranean. The Queen will proceed to Denmark later on, and it is hoped meanwhile that the Royal party will greatly benefit by the holiday on the sea. Their Majesties will have a very busy season to go through after Easter, as two or three Courts will be held before Whitsuntide, and there will also be a great deal of Royal entertaining both at Windsor and Buckingham Palace daring the next few months. The King's Visit to Bowood.—ln June, the Ring is to pay a visit to Lord and Lady Lansdowne at Bowood Park in Wiltshire. Bowood cannot boast of so many royal visits as some historic seats, such as Knowsley, or Chatsworth, but it is one of the "show places" of the county, and it was where Lord and Lady Lansdowne, who, before her marriage was Lady Maud Hamilton, ! spent their honeymoon some six and thirty years ago. The society of the sixties seems ancient history, but at that time the late Duke and Duchess of Abercorn were entertaining largely at Chesterfield House, giving balls, dinners and croquet parties' surrounded by their seven sons and seven daughters. All the Hamilton girls made ! brilliant marriages, and one of the great events of the ! mid-Victorian period was the double wedding of Lady Maud, and her sister Lady Albertha, now Lady Bland- ford, which took place in .Westminster Abbey in November, 1869. Lady Maud was considered one of the prettiest and most gifted of this remarkable set of sisters, of,whom she is the youngest. History repeats itself in Me Hamilton family, as regards brilliant marriages, and one of Lady Lansdowne's two daughters is Lady Waterford, whilst the other is Lady Evelyn Cavendish, the future Duchess of Devonshire. The Prince and Princess of Wales.—The Prince and Princess of Wales invariably spend Easter at Sandring- ham, but owing to His Royal Highness's recent indis- position, it is probable that the Prince and Princess will (spend the holidays at Frogmore Lodge, near Windsor, with their children. In the beginning of June their Royal Highnesses are to proceed to Berlin to represent the King and Queen at the wedding of the German Crown Prince, and already the arrangements are in a forward state for the visit to India, in the autumn. Among others who have been invited to accompany the Prince and Princess are Lord and Lady Shaftesbury. Lord Shaftesbury, like his gifted sister Lady Maud Warrender is very musical, land has a fine tenor voice. His wife is a sister of the Duke of West- minister, and a daughter of Lady Grosvenor. Presentation Gifts for We rships.—The Marchioneas of Ormonde is to christen and launch the new battle- ship "Hibernia" on June 19th, and meanwhile she is g etting up a subscription in Ireland for a presentation of plate, andl also a flag and ensign !for the vessel. Several of the newer warships, bearing county and colonial names, have received similar gifts from the ladies of leading families connected with the district, and only recently the residents of New Zealand made some handsome gifts to the battleship named after that distant colony, the flaeand ensign for the "Hibernia." are to be worked by the Royal Irish School of Art Needlework, and Lady Ormonde wishes to raise £l,OOO for the presentation plate which is to be entirely of Irish manufacture. The Marchioness is a great lover of all things pertaining to the sea, RS are her daughters, Lady Pole-Carew and Lady Constance Butler, and she is as devoted to yachting as her husband, the Marquis of Ormonde, who is Commodore of the Royal Yacht Squadron. Conversational Openings.—Lady Warwick has divided Society into two sections—those who bore and those who are bored. In most things we have improved, as in dress, manners, tastes, and culture, but, according to Lady Warwick and many other critics, the art of con- versation has gone, like the days of chivalry. People do not talk, they chatter, and, if we are to believe a lady's journal which recently suggested the pressing need of a handbook on "Conversational openings," they cannot even do that. There are times when speech fails, when the young man making a ceremonial call would perhaps give half-a-crown for an idea to talk abotat, but there are already books of the kind suggested, if he thinks they would help him. It is doubtful, hoverer, if they would give a greater variety of views and language, and it may be questioned whether there is any truth in all the talk about the decay of conversation. It would probably be nearer the mark to say that if there is any decay at all, it is in the art of listening, hut in any event it would be strange if, now-a-days, people were at a loss for conversation when there are so many more subjects of interest, alike to men and men and women, than was formerly the base. A Wise Old Saying.—The recent cold snan which drove the majority of us hack into our warmest winter garments and furs, brings home very forcibly the old saying " Ne'er Cast a Clout, till May is out." Warm underwear should be retained RS long as possible, and our outdoor costumes regulated according to the temperature. The few venturesome spirits who per- sisted in airing their new spring toilettes on those bitterly cold dais, are probably now regretting such a procedure, and are possibly making wiser resolutions for the future,

Concerning Furs.—The purchase of new furs is always a momentous matter, and as furs will be at their cheapest in a few weeks time from now, those among us con- templating an outlay in this direction would do well to carefully consider the subject. There is little doubt that all furs will be dearer than ever when autumn comes round again, and dough one runs a risk of being a little behind the times as regards style, when pur- chasing in June, the saving in price is considerable and alterations are very easily effected. Sable is still, and will be, first in favour and price, chinchilla coming second. American marten is in great request and will undoubtedly be exceedingly fashionable next season. while silver fox, blue fox, and sea otter, all commanded high prices at lithe spring wholesale, sales in London, at which an enormous advance in the price of squirrel was secured. Those women who store their furs at home cannot do better than first beat and brush them, then lay them in brown paper begs, securely gummed round, and in which should be placed a large handful of white carbon, obtainable for a few pence at all chemists. The tags should then be gummed up,and laid in a tin box,a quantity of the carbon being thrown loosely about itside. The bravest moth will decline to enter such an atmosphere, and when the furs are hung in the open air, the odour disappears in a few hours. Expensive Gloves.—Long gloves are a necessary accompaniment to the three quarter sleeve, and the fashionable outfitters are taking the opportunity to introduce several forms of extravagance into these in- dispensable articles of the toilette. Many of the newest gloves for outdoor wear are inset with lace, from the wrist to the elbow, the lace in some instances being ornamented with little glittering paillettes of gold,steel, or mother of pearl. Others have a long velvet Cavalier cuff, decorated with gold thread embroidery, whilst many of the new gloves depend upon the broderie Anglaise for their ornamentation. The pattern is punched through, and has a backing of a different shade to that of the glove, designed tn match the dress. All these styles are expensive, audit cannot he said that the fashionable three quarter sleeve makes for economy in the matter of gloves. Bridesmaids' Presents.—At several of the fashionable weddings arranged to take place between Easter and May, the bridegroom is presenting the bridesmaids with bouquets only, the brooch of interlaced monograms, and the chain bangle having outlived their vogue. Where the number of the" Maids " runs into two figures, as is now usually the case, the tax upon the bridegroom is a heavy one, and many prospective brides have wisely decided to abandon it.

Warrington P.S.A. Society. IMr. J. :Morton presided at an open meeting of this society held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, on Sunday. Miss Mansell contributed the two ! solos "Have you any room for Jesus" and "I have read of a beautiful city" very effectively, being accom- panied on the piano by Mr. B. Wadsworth. The Rev. C. L. Stowe spoke upon "The flowers of life." He dwelt orrthe great opportunities which are thrown away, and likened them to the story of the child who sat on a bridge with a flowing stream beneath her, plucked the Rowers one by one from the bunch which she held in her hand and let them sail away down the stream and when all were gone she wished she had thorn back again. He advised them to stick fast to the flower of opportunity and all would be well, to live a good life, for it was far better than being a prodigal and having to start over again. He asked all to be Christians at the risk of everything, and keep theirhoaghts and actions pure.

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
IN A SPRING-GARDEN,
SIR LEWIS MORRIS ' (Author of" The Epic of Hades," de.).

The yearly miracle is once ,?tnore being accom- plished. Spring with its flew hopes and mys- terious renewal, its disappointments and delays, Its cruel nipping winds anti frosts, is again here. Yet it is to its bright sun and lengthening days that we chiefly turn, its promise of a high summer which no doubt will be fulfilled in due time, though there may be yet long weeks of dismal days between us and it and it will very likely disappoint U 8 when it, comes. just as we are disappointed with the tardy honours and prizes of middle life. But at present all is pro- mise, and hope blossoms, like the outer world, for young lives and old, every flower that blooms is a new birth, to be " tenderly guarded and caredf or on account of its weak- ness and charm, tqs is a, ,young child. Later on, when the old world seems a mass of blossom and the springing 'hedges are hidden by perfect constellations of primroses and violets, and the woods are gay with anemones and blue•bells, and the meadows golden with buttercups, there is hardly the same delight in renewal, as is produced by the first snowdrop or crocus peep• tug through the grass. The year has come to its lusty growth, beautiful indeed, but komewhat arrogant too, and self-sufficient, rejoicing hi its rude strength, like the growing boy. Yet it is always beautiful, as is high summer itself, when the birds' songs are hushed, and the thick- leaved woods "make for themselves a cooling covert," and the haymaker whets his scythe, and treads at every step through wonders of crestect grasses and lovely flowers undreatnt of a few reeks back. Just now the thrushes are waking the whole country side with a perfect riot of formless melody. It is pleasant to walk through the woods and search for the first violet and

primrose shyly ..peeping forth from the carpet of dead leaves. ' Renewal " is what they preach with clamorous insistence, " Renewal. Resurrection, the Easter tide of Nature," like that of our mortal life, which will have its winter, • and will lie hidden too, "till like a clarion note the Spring shall sound " as a verse; writer of my acquaintimce has it. No man cares for them nor gives thein shelter, yet like the birds .and the bees who are in like case, they come forth when the sun calls them, prepared for another chequered year of homely- cares and pleasures, some withering when slimmer comes, all ending with winter at last. Ido not believe that. mankind will lose their great Hope while the world lasts, and is renewed, and clothes it- self with glory and brightness year after rolling year.

div.head: FILEFAILING FOIL SPRING.
div.p: FILEFAILING FOIL SPRING.

Just at present it is in the carefully tended glass houses that the first files of the advancing pageant arc most fully seen. I know nothing pleasanter than the air of such a place, not un- duly warm or damp ; not devoted to the un- canny orchid; which spells death to so many honest lads who coine out at • dawn from the reeking heat to be stricken with death by the cruel east wind. But in a house facing due aouth, w th only a moderate artificial warmth— to assist the growing heat of the returnine. sun ; the prospect just now is enchanting. The vines are just starting into pale leaf, making ready for the time when the lithe canes shall stretch cut and the tendrils wind round every possible support, and the curiously insignificant green Lowers expand with that delicious vinous bou- quet, which very few notice, but which is as powerful as that of the little red tufts, on the larches a month or so later. It was at a great Yorkshire house with acres of glass that I first experienced the charm of the subtle odour to which an old friend and poet—the late Lord Houghton—directed my attention. He quoted, I remember, a line from his own poems, which at this moment I forget, but which proved that he had long been familiar with the scent. , Look- ing with the eye of imag,4nation, one can see the bore rods, laden with the heavy purple bunches which have played so large a part in the story of man, and will again : but it is in the peach house that there is the tenderest yet most lavish display of innocent gaiety of colour. Roof and walls are alike covered with a pink cloud of the exquisite blossoms of peach and • • nectarine. They are waiting a little anxiously, it would seem, for the honey-bees, who alas ! have not come yet, chilled and torpid from the past weeks of frost. Very soon now there will come a fine warm morn- ing when the gay suitors, newly wakened, will wing their way through the windows opened to the balmy air, and the hum of life will be every- where, and the blossoms will fall and the fruit begin to gather in their stead. The oranges mid the lemons too arc beginning to feel the force of the spring, and to break out with those curiously minute shoots and flower buds which very soon will fill the house • with their per- fume. The azaleas are already hidden in bloom. The cyclamens, white and purple, are at their best, lifting up, on Tong slender stalks, their coronets of graceful flowers. Outside, the lawns are studded with crocuses yellow, white and purple, which, spriugiug from 11. e short grass, remind one irresistibly of the- Sicilian meadows where Persephone, wandering with her gay com- panions, long long ago, was snatched away by her lover, the King of the unseen realms, to bear mile over the dead. Renewal, Restitution, Resurrection, this is the universal voice, which sounds everywhere from the awakened world.

SUMMER'S piton:snug. • Perhaps, as I have said, here and elsewhere, this sense is not so vivid later on, when every hedge-row and covert, fs bright with anemones and golden celandines, pale with primroses or blue with wild hyacinth, and be starred later still with pink lychnis, and • the enamelled white of the stitchwort and blue of the speedwell, and the hawthorn. and virginal cherry and pear, and apple nita lilac and luburnam make the world a thing of unmixed and almost cloying beauty and delight. But it will be then no longer a place of wonder as it is now, but of fruition, deep but, alas, not complete, material splendours dulling the . spiritual sense : as they do in the full flush of successful manhood. It is rather by the fugitive nature of these charms that we are impressed, looking for- ward, half impatiently, with a certain sense of satiety, to the time' When these vain and lav- ish shows shall be done, and sober Autumn shall have come with its wealth of harvest-tide to crown the Year of our life with a content which ii d •ed it will hardly bring. But how bright n eaawhile and splendid is the pageant of stun- tiler. There is not a square foot on the lawn or meadow so bare and monotonous now and dis- figured still with last year's dead leaves, that will not be transformed into as beautiful garden ground, lit with a hundred gay blossoms and grasses which no husbandman's hand ever 'sowed. When at length the queenly rose appears with the crown of midsummer , sweetness and grace, and the pansies with their innocent childlike eyell and faces, and a score of others are lighting the parterres of the garden, it seems as if nothing was wanting to complete the picture of ,beauty. But we must not forget the rhodo- dendrons ; great masses- of varied blossom, of almost every shade of colour. which precede and proclaim the coming of their kinswoman the Queen. Twenty years ago I planted them in congenial peat soil in great numbers, and now they are front April to July, in every year, a delight to the eye us they mount blossomed to the top, a blaze of colour against the bright blue sky. Nor that surest sign of high summer. the vestal lotus of the fish ponds, white or pink, or golden, rising like a jewel from amidst its broad- pread leaves.

div.head: STRIKING CONTRAST.
div.p: A STRIKING CONTRAST.

I am afraid all these. simple pleasures will seem sadly vapid and unattractive, not to say effeminate to those who • are devotees of what la known tiS " sport," the survival of the primi- Eve instincts of flamgliter, necessary for the savage man, no doubt, and on which the whole fabric of modern society still rests, but some• anomalous, if not ridiculous, whcre the

poulterer is well established and prospers. These violent delights are for the young —whether in years or undeveloped intellect. and the absence of that pity for the weak mid suffering which seems, in the male at any rate, only the precious possession of Age. Some of these days one would hope, young Englishmen of high birth and breeding will be ashamed to send to the papers glowing accounts of the massacre of thousands of harmless and unresisting little birds and beasts, accomplished between a late breakfast and afternoon tea, with, an interval for hot luncheon between, and a luxurious dinner to follow. Probably one would- think the chase of the wily fox will fall into disuse too. But here a doubt takes one. That is the use of crying Peace, where no peace is, when in fact, the whole con- stitution of nature, and of man rests upon bloodshed and force ? Think of the immense mass -or autumn and animal sullermr-, wit.,:tt Lt. is in the power of an ignorant old Dtil farmer to ensure by a fatuous application to his own .very different case of the promises to the Hebrews against the Amalekites. How are such fanatic-isms to be met with suceess, unless our young peo- ple are taught, like the Persians of old, to shoot and to ride, and not to shrink from bloodshed and death, whether for themselves or others ? No 1' it is of no use ignoring facts. It is pos- sible to be so full of the peaceful aspects of nature as to ignore the ceaseless warfare on which it is based. It is necessary perhaps that the growing animal, and the growing nation, if it is to do its destined wolk in the world, should have sterner work to do titan Epicurean pleasures, however innocent in themselves.

THE EVENING'S REST. But for those whose work in the world is well nigh done, there is no fitter pleasure than that which comes from the garden. A charming book "In Praise of Gardens," published a couple of years back, from which I have before quoted with profit, in an essay under that title, brings this out witn peculiar force. The author has brought together an extraordinary collection of passages from great writer a of all ages and countries, all concurring in this, that the great- est pleasure of Age is the contemplation and cultivation of Nature as shown in her yearly pageant of flowers and fruits, " 'Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these,' and in all his wisdom," says Southey, describing a flower garden, " never taught more wholesome lessons than these silent monitors convey to a thoughtful mind and an understanding heart." " There are two books," says Sir Thomas Brownie, " from whence I collect my Divinity; besides that written one of God, another of his servant Na- ture, that universal and public manuscript that lies expanded unto the eyes of all. Those that never saw Him in the one have discovered Him in the other. Surely the heathen knew better ' how to join and read these mystical letters than we who cast a more careless eye on those com- mon hieroglyphics and disdain to suck divinity from the flowera of nature." "I look upon the whole country in spring-time as a spacious gar- den, and make as many visits to a spot of daisies or a bank of violets, as a florist does to his borders or parterres. There is not a bush in blossom within a mile of me, which I am not acquainted with, nor scarce a daffodil or cowslip that withers away in my neighbourhood with- out my missing it." That is what Joseph Ad- dison says in one of his letters to Mr. Specta- tor, and it seems to me that it is the right atti- tude of mind for one like him who has retired from the active cares and struggles of life to the tranquil delights of the country. "To this complexion all must come at last. It is rather a shock at first if you feel that your powers of brain and your strength of body afe still undi- minished to find that room must be made never- theless for younger people. It is npt that one is not happy in retirement. The delights of society, the cares of politics, the bustle of 'town, even the charms of art or the theatre no longer allure. " Jam in my garden and shoot strong and tenacious roots," says the old werdling Boling- broke writing to Dean Swift; " I have caught hold of the earth, to use a gardener's phrase, and neither my friends nor my enemies will find it an easy matter to transplant me again." Nor is the feeling peculiar in this age to old statesman. "De- vote your energies if you are wise to municipal life." said Lord Rosebery a year ago at Swansea " The worst of a seat in Parliament is that it involves your tunning your backs, upon the country, when it is that full flush and beauty of summer which is the best gift of the Creator to men." But for the delights of gal- loping furiously after a rank, smell all the win- ter long, which, while there are Boers who mis- apply the Books of Chronicles and Kings to be dealt with, must, lam afraid go on, the complaint of the great lady, that she had never seen her own roses blossom would be no longer heard. We should pity the poor rich for whom so great a source of innocent pleasure is only to be en- joyed by snatches, on week-end visits from the stifling town, or at a time when the best of the pageant is over for the year.

the Commission further stated could be raised end maintained only on the principle that it was the duty of every citizen of military age and sound physique to Ibe trained for national defence. Illhat the National Service League proposed was simply an addition to the education of the youth of the country who out, in the interests of the community,to be trained to the use of arms That scheme differed entirely from conscription which meant the taking of men frotnCivil life, locking them up in barracks, and making them professional soldiers witm anti-civilian instincts. One of the best ways of fighting physical deterioration, which presented a very vital danger and more or less threatened us with natiousf decay, was to go in for universal trainiug. lire ought to- do our best to make the children in the schools physi- ming fit, so that when they were called upon to undergo military training it would not be a question of " filling them out and stiffening them up.' (Elear, hear.) The sacrifices necessary for home defence should be under- taken b} all instead of by the few as at present. Every man should be prepared to assist in the defence of our common country and our common rights. (Applause)" The Rev. W. BRACECAMP moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Quelch and said he supported the League's pro- posals because he was a man of peace, and believed that the right way to sscure peace a-as that everyone should be trained as a soldier and be able to fight. Universal training would also do much to improve the physique of the nation. Mr. GEORGE DALE seconded and said the system which the league ad vocated was thoroughly democratic, and the burden would be borne equally by all. England had much to fear from the spirit of lethargy, and he contended that had that same spirit been manifested by our forefathers there would have been no British empire to. defend.

• The resolution was heartily agreed to. Mr. Qura.crf, in responding, said he was against con- scription, but conscription and universal military train- ing 'were wide as fithe poles assunder. The most re- actionary Conservative and the most extreme Socialist ought to be prepared to agree that the best thing they could work for ins State was a great people—physically mentally and morally—a free, happy and prosperous people. By supporting the League's proposals he be- lieved they 'would be furthering those most desirable conditions. Mr. J. H. SMETHURST moved a vote of thanks to tha chairman. Captain G. R. CROSFIELD seconded and appealed for active co-operation in the great task of forming public opinion on the subject. The political weathercocks were just waiting to see which way the breeze was going to blow. Warrington was the first town to organize any utterance in favour of compulsory service,and Manchester and Liverpool were now following suit. (Applause). The vote was heartily accorded, and Mr. Roberts acknowledged the compliment. lie was particularly glad that a leader of workingmen's opinion like Mr. , Quelch had had the courage to tell them what very few leaders of tbe workingmen had had the courage to tell them—what in their own interests and the interests of the country it was their duty to do on that question.

This column. of cycling gossip will appear every week from the present time till the end of the cycling season. It will be different from anything of the kind that has ever appeared in any paper outside the cycling press. In writing it I shall be assisted by some of the best writers on cycling subjects and by experts of many years' experience in cycling and journalistic matters. It will be illustrated—not simply with advertising cuts from catalogues, but with our own artists' sketches, as well as technical drawings to illustrate technical subjects. It will be full of features interesting attractive, and useful to those who ride bicycles and those who hope to do so. In this first letter only a general outline of the many interesting subjects to be dealt with can.be given, and if any readers want information on other points at any time, they have only to send a letter addressed to the Cycling Editor expressing their wishes, and they will receive attention. The Season's Prospects " Distinctly indicate that there will be in 1905 a greater increase in the popularity of cycling among the great masses of the people than we have ever yet seen. Recent reductions in price have had a highly stimulating effect in increasing the volume of business in bicycles. Cycle manu- facturers as a rule are extremely busy, and in some instances the March trade is running into record figures as regards numbers of machines, though prices and profits are lower than ever before. Cycles are now within the reach of all, and Provided purchasers do not go too far in their demands for a low price, no one need hesitats
patronize the bicycles of good names and reputations which are now being offered at figures that would have been quite impossible a year or two back.

Thoroughly reliable bicycles for boys and girls at six guineas or even less are one of the features of the present season, and a few more shillings Will obtain for the adult rider a sound reliable machine complete with free wheel, two rim brakes, and the necessary detail improvements, which make the bicycle of to-day such a safe and .pleasurable means of locomotion.

Those who go to eight or ten gm__ may obtain a cycle equal or superior to the twelve and fifteen-guinea bicycles of two or three yea. 7 ago. Row have all these reductions in price come about? To some small extent owing to the expiry of tyre patents and the cheapening of tyres, but !argely owing to the increasing use of machinery ta the production of cycle parts, and this has become possible owing to the fact that recent changes in fashion have not altered the main features of the standard pattern of bicycle.
BY THE CLUBMAN.

div.head: MR. H. QUELCH ADVOCATES .COMPULSORY SERVICE AS THE REMEDY.
div.p: MR. H. QUELCH ADVOCATES .COMPULSORY SERVICE AS THE REMEDY.
Mating In Parr Hall,

"The Muddle of Military Reform and the Way Out " was the subject of an address delivered in the Parr Hall, Warrington, on Monday evening, coder tne auspices of the National Service League, by Mr. H. .Quelch, the well-known social leader. ! The attendance was some- what meagre, Mr. Henry Roberts presiding. A letter of apology for non-attendance was received from the Rector.

In his introductory remarks the CHAIRMAN said he was sorry they could not muster a larger audience to discusa a question of such great national importance. When he remembered the large audiences which met together (luring the time of the Boer war—a time when perhaps we realized more vividly than we had realised since, the extreme gravity of the situation—it was disappointing to some extent to feel that because we were now out of the difficulty which then appeared to face us for the time being, the matter had not sufficient interest for us. However, if they only just looked back upon the history of the country and retnembered bow many great causes began in a very much smaller way than the National Service cause had begun, they might take heart, knowing that the clay would surely come when the principles which they believed were absolutely necessary for the safeguarding of the interests of the homeland and the empire would be compelled to be put in active operation. He thought the paucity of numbers that night was not to be attributed to any large amount of virulent opposition, hut rather to Ur+ fact, which was so characteristic of the English people, that until they were stirred up with a long pole they were content to let things alone. After the revelations of the War Cornmissioh, which had shown lus in what a state of absolute necessity we stood, after ' the revelations of the committee which had been in- quiring into the physical conditions of the young people of this country, one would have thought that many more would have attended a meeting of that kind to see how far the proposals of the League were calculated to meet either or both of those serious matters. The oftener the proposals were discussed, the sooner would come the time when the majority of people would be convinced of their necessity and reasonableness. The proposals were that every youth who was physically fit should at the. age of eighteen have two or three months training in camp, and for two or three years following that he should have at least a fortnight's similar training ; the object being simply that in the event of an attack upon us—the army being in all pro bability required for the defence of various part of the empire—we should have at our call, if necessary, a large number of men not simply willing to defend our shores, because every Englishman was ready to Jo that, but capable of taking a man and a soldier's part in such defence. He had no adequate words in which to I express his contempt for the man who was willing to take,at the expense of others, all the protection,comfort and convenience which we as Englishmen enjoyed, and who was not prepared to do his share in maintaining these conditions andihelping ,to hand them down to future generation& (Applause). Mr. QCELCH, in dealing with military muldle, said that if they talked to continental military experts about the British army, they wanted to know where it was. (Laughter). Looking civet the history of this country since the Boer war, it seemed to him that we had simply gone on muddling in the direction of what had been called reform, and so far from reforming anything and securing a more efficient force for national defence, we had only made "confusion worse confounded." The expenditure on the army was constantly increasing, till at present £l5Bl per annum for every soldier in the ranks was being I spent. A number of schemes had been promulgated by different war ministers, the latest by Mr. Arnold Forster, but nobody had been able to discover what that gentle-. 1 man was driving at. (Laughter.) The only thing they were able to discover was that small as the noun- hers of the regular army (200,000) were, they were to be reduced, the volunteers were to be discouraged, and the militia was to be rendered available for foreign service. Mr. Arnold Forster said there was no evidence to show that the—army was, either in composition or numbers, the army which was really required to satisfy the peculiar needs of the empire. The physical standard for regular soldiers of eighteen, continued Mr. Quelch, was 21 inches below the height and 151bs. below the weight of the average boy of seventeen. The National Service League advocated as a way out of the muddle not conscription but universal military train- ing for all the youth of the country. He advocated it, because as a workman and a social democrat, he was an ardent lover of peace, and he believed the proposals of the League to be the‘best and surest guarantee of intetnational peace. That was the opinion of the great- est political party in the civilized world—the great social democratic party which was the only international party, a,fd was at one in sup- porting the proposal of universal training on those grounds. Not only was preparedness for war the best guarantee of peace, but they believed that the best way to " seek peace and ensue it " was to bring the consequences of war home to the whole of the people. It was urged that universal training was calculated to instil a spirit of militarism and jingoism in the minds of the people, but he believed the very contrary to be the case. At the time of the Boer War— which he and the party to which he belonged regarded as a crime and a blunder—it was not the men who had to go out and fight who were the worst jingoes, but the people who sat at home idle and in ease while the fighting was being done for them. Universal training also tended to a greater consciousness of national responsibility, and was, he believed, tke best way of (mewing freedom. To talk about universal dis- armament Eir even the reduction of armaments under present circumstances was to cry "Peace, peace," where .0 peace was. As far as the social democratic party was concerned it was opposed to the maintenance of stand- ing armies. The members of that body said that the standing armies could be done away with, but that the skeleton of military orgaalza- Con should be retained, and all the men in the country should be properly drilled and collected for mobilization ready for national defence at home or abroad. Every man should be a citizen, and every citizen should have a rifle and know how to use it as well against any attempt at despotism at home as any attempt at invasion from abroad. The recent Com- mission which inquired into the state of the auxiliary forces found that those forces had neither the strength nor military efficiency required to fulfil the functions for which they existed. An army for defence purposes

div.head: " THRO' FIRE AND WATER."
div.p: " THRO' FIRE AND WATER."

Dramatic Entertainment by Crosfield's Workpeople. Messrs. Crosfield's workpeople have taken another step in the direction of social entertainment. Some months ago it was suggested in a jocular spirit that a works dramatic society should be formed. The proposal , was afterwards considered seriously, and the first fruits were forthcoming last week end, in the production in the work's assembly room of the comic drama " Thro' Fire and Water." Of the play itself little need be sale. Of the ordinary type of melodrama, the principal characters were an hero, an injured heroine and an unsuccessful villain. The hero, who, as is usual, is poor but ittrictly honest, has at con- siderable peril to himself rescued the heroine from a fire when she was a child of tender years: De naturally falls in love with her and after a period Of indecision and misunderstanding learns that she has the highest regard for him. The heroine was of the tearful order whose identity is unknown save to the aristocractic villiau who strives, but in vain to prevent her entering into possession of the wealth which rightly belongs to her. In his endeavonrs tbe villian is assisted by one like unto himself except that his:social standing is far different. The plottings of the two are exposed by a struggling artist whose work of discovery is inspired by the sister of the hero. In the first act all things combine to assist the villains in their endeavours but in the concluding scene wrong is defeated, right is established, and all ends happily, the curtain being rung down to the appropriate strains of a wedding march played by the orchestra. As to the acting, considering the inexperience of the players it was of a high order, and much better things can be expected in the future. Taking the characters in the order of merit Mr. W. Tynan, as "Mike Biddies" the minor villain, comes first. His acting was char- ft3terized with pleasing freedom and naturalness. The same can be said in praise of Itliss A. Shaw as "Honour Bright" sister of the hero. If she had one fault, how- ever, it was that her pronunciation was at times inaccurate. Mr. J. Newnes,as tbe hero," Joe Bright " Ives occasionally a little forced in his acting though otherwise little fault. could be found with his interpre- tation of the character. Mr. J. W. Spenseley, as " Kit Coventry," the struggling artist, was a distinct success, and as the villain Mr. F. Gartland was extremely well placed. Miss E. Derbyshire had a difficult part to pourtray as the heroine, and acquitted herself ably. Her only fault was that at times she failed to Mere sufficient spirit into her acting. Taken altogether the production was a success and well merited the heartily expressed appreciation of the large audiences which assembled both on Friday and Saturday evenings. Mr. T. Knowles was an efficient stage manager. In addition to the dramatic performance an excellent musical programme was submitted. The works quar- tette, Messrs. Tynan, Hignett, E. Walker, and H. Cook, were perhaps a little nervous but otherwise their singirm was excellent. Mr. E. Walker and Miss A.Cook were both responsible for songs and of each it might be said that while they sang well their singing lacked expression. Master H. Griffiths was heatrily encored for his contribution, giving in response " The Longshore- man." Mr. J. P. Ilignett was the humorist and succeeded ,in his endeavours to create mirth. Instrumental selec- tions were given by an orchestra composed mainly of the workpeople, who played well and fully merited the hearty reception which was accorded them.

Diagram 86 shows a very pretty fancy stroke which really further demonstrates the tendency of reverse rotation to bring the ball back to the striker. h-;.sir :ke is a screw cannon off two object balls on to a third object ball. The cue ball should be about 3 or 9 inches from the first object ball, and the four balls should form a kind of square. The stroke 'is played as though simply playing to cannon off the white ball on to the first red ball with a fairly fast stroke. If the cue ball catch the red ball as shown by the intersected circle, it ivill recoil more or less in the direction of the second red bail, the reason being that the contact with the first red ball stops the cue ball from travelling any further across the table; and this gives full play to the retrcgrade rotation which it still carries. In order for the shot to come off, the cue ball muSt not catch the fir.,t red ball very full nor very thin. The stroke is perhaps easier by placing the fourth ball a little out of the square as marked by the x on the diagram, for the cue- hall will often recoil in the direction shown by the intersected line. The stroke, however, looks most effective when the balls form a square. Last week, in discussing screw in-offs into a blind pocket, I referred to the tendency of check side to pull the ball away from the side cushion when playing for a baulk pocket right against the nap of the cloth, and stated that the beet way of nullifying the effect of the nap was to play the stroke with plenty of pace. In Diagram 87 the stroke (position A) is shows again in order to compare it with the similai lo6kingte3troke illustrated at B. Though the twe strokes look of a like nature, a considerabl,differ- ence exists between them, for whereas the in-on at A must be played with check side owing to the pocket being a very blind one, cheek side is not compulsory for the in-off at B, owing to the pocket being moderately open. In fact, it is better to play the in-off at B with running side (right-hand side in the Diagram), for the effect of this side against the nap of the cloth will pull the ball towards the pocket. When playing the stioke with running side, it is better to play as though trying to screw on to the lower shoulder of the pocket (the baulk cushion angle) in order to melte some allowance for the pull of fhe nap. By playing pith running side the pocket is ren- dered somewhat more open, as the cue-ball, aftet a slight swerve away from the pocket caused by the reverse rotation, pulls to the pocket again. The more slowly a successful stroke is Played flit

ana innaten it. By tnis ctevice tne aetay ay a paneture can be reduced to within two minutes. 01ley rode Constrictor tyres, which are particularly suitable for treatment in this way, but a spare inner tube of other makes of tyres could be carried this way, and I shall be much surprised if this dodge does not become a universal one among all who make attempts at lowering records.
