div.head: XXXII'.
div.p: XXXII'.
Screw and Reverse Rotation
(CONTINUED.)

Last week I referred to the curve which the cue ball often describes in. screw strokes. When an object ball is struck quite full, a screw will bring the cue ball straight back, but if the object ball be struck less than full the cue ball will always describe a more or less pronounced curve provided the stroke be played with strength and the cue ball be under the influence of strong re- verse rotation at the moment of contact. In order for the curve to be very pronounced the cue ball must be near the; object ball, for if it be any distance away its retrograde rotation will be more or, less exhausted before the object ball is struck.
DIAGRAM 85.

The screw cannon shown on Diagram 85—posi- tion A—is a fine example of the great sweeping curve that a cue ball sometimes makes in strong, screw strokes. The shot may look a fancy one Cu the diagram, but it is a good sound stroke, and one that is played by professionals in serious games. Cecil Harveson, who has no superior at strong screws oFten plays this cannon. The stroks requires plenty of power, and in the posiA tion shown on the diagram the object ball should be taken just a shade fuller than half-ball. The cue ball is thrown off very squarely, but almost immediately the strong retrograde rotation asserts itself, and causes the ball to swerve in a very pronounced manner. • The stroke is not really a difficult one to any player possessing strong screwing powers, but it is as well to play it with a little running side (lett hand side in the diagram) to ensure the cannon being made when the cue ball strikes the top cushion too far from the second object ball to permit of the cannon being made without side. Sometimes the curve may be so very pro- rounced that the cue ball cannons direct on to the second object ball without first striking the top cushion. • It might be thought by Many players that in order for the cue ball to describe a curve when playing a screw stroke the object ball must not be taken too thin. Such a rule, however, only hulds good when the cue ind object balls are some little distance apart. When instead they are quite close to each other, a distinct curve may result from the thinnest of contacts. This can easily be demonstrated by placing the balls in. some such position as shown at di on Diagram Si (cue and object ball only one inch apart). If the cue hall be struck low down and the object ball be taken quite thinly a cannon can be made without much difficulty and the swinging back of the cue ball will be plainly noticeable. Nor is much strength required, for owing to the cue ball being so close to the object ball it strikes it without any sensible loss of reverse rotation. --RAM '

div.head: Runcorn Rural District Council and the Election of Relieving Officer.
div.p: The Runcorn Rural District Council and the Election of Relieving Officer.

Sir,—ln a report of the meeting of the above Council it is stated that " Contrary to custom the Press was excluded from the meeting." Why this change in the mode of doing business? Have the Runcorn Guardians forgotten that they are elected by the public to watch their interests, and to do their work? Then why this secrecy ? Was there anything in connection with the candidates that would not bear the light ? or anything concerning the Guardians which was not regular—such as canvassing —that the election of a public officer to till a public office should be decided in camera ? Six of the applicants were asked to appear before the Board, each of them, and each of the Guardians knew that only one of the candidates could be successful; and both the candidates and the rate- payer expected that the Board without fear or favor would select him whom they deemed the fittest person. Was such the case ? If Mr. Pearson the selected candi- date was, independent of every other consideration thought to be the best man, then why in the name of all that is English, and open, and honest, should the Runcorn Guardians be afraid of the public knowing what was said and done at the election of Relieving oflicer ?—I am Sir, Yours obediently, A RATEPAYER.

Councillor Stott and the Next Election. Sir,—ln going carefully through "Nunqualm's" last letter I find that it is practically what he said in his first letter rgarding Councillor Stott, only in slightly different form and I gave him my answer which still holds good, namely, Mr. Stott is only doing his duty as a Labour man in helping Mr. Seddon and furthering the cause of the workers. Councillor Stott never stated he should" ignore "the issue of the next election, as" Nunqualm " states, but simply, that "ho should take no interest as far as act wit work was concerned," which is very different. I also note that" Nunqualm " has not brought a single argument against the principles set forth in my letters nor has he denied the charges I rnade against the principles of the Tory and Liberal parties of class legislation. He also omits to say anything shout the "practical christianity "of which r wrote. Now, this being so, leads me to think, that he agrees to a certain extent at least, with my ideas, and I make bold to ask him a straight question; if a Labour candidate had been in the field for Warrington, would he have supported him, if not, why not? He refers to our present Member of Parliament and says," he belongs to a party which,l believe, is not pro- moting the interests of the working classes—vide Pro- tection." Well." Nunqualm" my opinion is,that neither our present Member nor Mr. Crorfield would represent the working classes so well ass Labour candidate would do, although, I have nothing to say against either of the gentlemen named,so far as their personality is con- cerned, but the parties to which they belong do not truly represent the masses of workers. Would you ex- pect aTrades Unionist to invitehis employer to b come chairman of his Trade Society, I should say not, then why expect him to send employers, capitalists, and monopolists to Parliament to make laws governing him and the trade of his country on which he depends for his living ? Does it not seem reasonable to expect that a party consisting of employers, (lcc., will see that their interests are safe first when they are placed in a position to do so? You may say it is not reasonable, but it is nevertheless a fact. When working men will sink their old political differ- ences and combine in one strong Labour Party,then,and then only will they receive their due rights and be fairly and honestly represented in the House of Com- mons. At present the worker beats himself. To show what I mean by that, is this, a number of working men vote Liberal, others vote Conservative, and these two parties when in the " House " oppose each other vigor- ously. Therefore,you have one set of workers endeavour- ' ing to thwart what the others are trying to accomplish, the consequence is. that he (the worker) usually gets nothing, whereas, if those two sets of workers would combine and send one of their own class to directly represent them in Parliament, then, as I say, and then only, will his cause be voiced. Yours &c., " FAIRPLAY." April 11th, 1905.

div.head: Premature Burial.
div.p: Premature Burial.

Sir,—lt will, I suppose, be generally agreed that the thought of awaking from a sleep which has been mis- taken for death and finding oneself doomed to suffocation in a coffin, is one of the most horrible with which the human mind can be haunted. And yet under our present lax law of death certification and burial, this is a fate to which every one is more or less liable. A clear proof of this may be found in the very narrow escapes from live burial by which ever andanon the public is shocked. One comparatively recent case is that of Sirs. Holden, of Accrington, who was laid out for dead, and a death certificate given, a copy of which I have before me whilst writing. And in a book I have before me entitled "Premature Burial and how it may be prevented," by William Tebb, F.R.G.S. and Colonel Edward Perry M.D., Late Medical Inspector U.S. Army,many such narrow escapes in our own and othei countries are , recorded; whilst opened vaults and upturned grave- I yards have furnished unequivocal evidence of some terrible past-burial death struggles. But such sad occurrences need scarcely excite surprise on reflecting that although some kinds of suspended animation so exactly simulate death that trained observers may be deceived, that even experts are often unable to decide whether the boundary line between life and death has been passed. Yet the law allows death certifi- cates to be given and burials to take place on the mere hearsay evidence of relatives or friends,and without met:tics' examination of the alleged dead person or the verification of actual death by its only infallible sign—putrefactive and decomposition. As Dr. W. R. Hadwen has said : "The law protects the citizen's life,property,and every other interest up to the moment when the death scene supervenes; then it leaves him, and provides no protection whatever against mistakes which may be made at this supreme crisis." But should not htunan life be regarded as too sacred to be thus endangered by any preventible mistakes ? There can scarcely be a greater disideratum than that sought by the London Association for the Prevention of Pre- mature Burial, viz., that of effecting such a reform of the law as will render such awful catastrophes as live sepulture impossible,and they deserve the support of all classes in this philanthropic work. Yours faithfully, J. WEST.

div.head: Bradford-on-Avon. April llth, 1905.
div.p: Bradford-on-Avon. April llth, 1905.

Sir,—A Bill is, I believe, being introduced in Parlia- ment to amend the law in this matter. Such a Bill having for its aim the prevention of premature burial is well worthy of serious consideration and ought not to be passed over even if it does not make much progress before this Parliament. That premature burials do occur is not to be doubted and we cannot help suspect- ing that they happen much more frequently than is generally b?lieved. The horrors of a premature burial must be terrible, and it is a duty of mankind to avoid needless suffering by mutual co-operation and by intelli' gent scientific investigation. No doubt it is consoling for its to say when a person is dead (or is supposed to be dead) that it is the will of God, hut should that person be prematurely interred is it still the will of God (assuming that God exists and is all-known) that such a person should suffer that fate? If it is the will of God, by supporting the Measure referred to we are directly opposing God's will. How- ever, if God does not see fit to prevent premature interment, of necessity it remains for us, as it has always done during the course of evolution (natural evolution), to make a shift for ourselves. The Bill, which has been prepared by the London Society for the Prevention o. Premature Burial, provides (according to one of our daily papers) "that there shall be no burial or disposal of a body without a medical certificate of death, that no such certificate shall be given without a personal inspection and examination of the body, and that the certificate shallow.° the signs from which death is inferred. If a body is buried in defiance of the Act, not only are the parties concerned liable to punishment, but power is given to a Justice of the Peace to order the exhumation of the body improperly buried." These orders strictly carried out and enforced would materially assist in removing present defects and would reduce to it minimum any chances of fraud where persons, whose lives are insured; die under suspicious circumstances. In this direction and by making it almost impossible for a person to be buried alive the measure will do good if passed, and undoubtedly the public ought to see that it is passed sooner than later.—Yours truly, W.. 11 BELL, Jun., 38, Bewsey-street, Warrington.

The incident of which the above discussion arose was referred to at the March Council meeting by Alderman Tinnion who related a conversation he had been told of which took place between a certain gentleman and a member of the Town Council. The two men met at a railway station and the Councillor said to the other " Get in here, I Want to say something to you." When they got in he said " Now we are by ourselves I have something to say. I make a proposal to you, and if it is carried through you give me £100." " Why don't you do it ?" said the gentleman. "Oh, lam a member of the Town Council, end I cannot," was the reply. " But, it is a funny proposal to make." " Well," continued the other, "If I start this proposal will you give me £lOO if it is carried through ?' The gentleman then said" I would like to denounce you," but the Colincillor replied, " Ah, but there are only us two in the compartment and my word is as good as yours." That showed, concluded Councillor Tinnion, how things could be done.

The great strength of Free Trade, continued Mr. Maddison, was not merely that it had cheapened food, but that it had widened the choice of the poor in the articles which they could eat. Mr. Chamberlain said he would not tax raw material, but an arrangement like that could not go on. The dissatisfaction created in the Colonies would be so great that raw material would inevitably come to have its preference and therefore an increased price. Then, as to TRE DIFFICULTY OF DEFINING RAW MATERIAL, it must be remembered that what was the manufactured article:to one maulwas only the raw!material to a person engaged in another branch of industry. The advantages of raw material were really the crux of the industrial problem. For Heaven's sake,let them keep the bands of the tax imposer off raw materials! Mr. Chamberlain said we were being ruined because manufactured goods were imported in such great quantities. He said that if we exported goods instead of importing them, the country would be happy and prosperous. There was an increase in the importation of manufactured goods in 1904 as compared with the previous year of less than three-quarters of a million, whereas there was au increase in the exportation of manufactured goods of over nine millions. div.head: BOROUGH BUDGET.
div.p: THE BOROUGH BUDGET.
A TWOPENNY REDUCTION IN THE RATES.
Municipal Expenditure Not Due to Extravagance.

By approving the Borough Budget on Tuesday evening the Warrington Town Council sanctioned the levying of a total rate of 7s. Bd. in the --ta reduction of twopeuce on the rate for the past year. As usual the duty of presenting the Budget, which has already been summarised in the "Examiner," I devolved upon Alderman Fai,clough as chairman of the ' Finance Committee. His statement was as follows : Before presenting the Budget, I should like to sly a few words about the estimates of last year. It is satisfactory to be able to note that the Borough Rate Account has been closed with only £l5 is. 7d. due to the bankers. (Hear, heir.) This means that, speaking generally, the departments as a whole have kept fairly within their estimates. The only committee which need be mentioned is the General Purposes, which has I exceeded its estimate by £1,130, having paid £2,632 for / Parliamentary and legal expenses, mainly due to the Ship Canal action, whilst only £1,200 was provided for. As a set-off against this, the Baths, Cemetery and Finance Departments are within their expenditure, and the receipts Live exceeded the anticipated amount. (Hear, hear.) In the Improvement Rate there has been considerable diversity between the estimates and the amounts received and paid, but the general result has been that the year has closed with a credit of £551 15s. Gd. The only items that call for notice are those of the Hospital and Health Departments, which, owing to the prolonged epidemic o scarlet fever necessitated an overspending of £1,500. Against this, the Sanitary Works Departments are within their estimates by £6OO, and there was also a larger amount received from the Gas Department than was estimated, which has helped to bring about the credit balance. With reference to the Budget, the total sum required is £1,328 less than last year, and this will enable the rates to be reduced by 2d. in the £. It appears on the face of this that the rates should be re- duced by 4c1., but the 4s. 2d. rate leviect last year for poor rate was not sufficient to meet the requirements, the difference having to be made up out of the Over- seers' working balance. It is interesting to note that with the exception of the item of .£2OO for branch libraries, there has not been any necessity to deleteany item from the estimates as presented, as was done last ' year. Having arrived at this satisfactory paint, I hope that each committee will again carefully avoid exceeding their extimates and will periodi- cally examine the details of their departments to see , that due economy is being exercised. Examining the I Budget in detail, the expenditure on Borough Rate Account apart from the question of balances is £3,172 in excess of last year. Of that sum the Watch Depertment are responsible for £4l3,mainly due to the appointment of extra constables and a larger amount to be spent on the police buildings. The general Purposes Committee require 2480 more, £l,OOO having been added to Partia- -1 mentary Expenses Account for the Ship Canal Action,but the sum set aside last year for Non-Trading Inquiry expenses is not again required. The Finance Depart- ment is £1,i67 more, 21,000 being again re-instated for Parliamentary expenses, as it is desirable that this item should be paid off as soon as possible; the amounts for salaries and interest on amount spent in O:CWI3 of sanctions being the other principal items. The Educa- tion Committee also require £1,407 more than last year. In the Improvement Rate the expenditure is £2,200 more, due to the fact ofj the requirement of the whole of the committees whose expenses are chargeable to this account, being slightly in excess of last year. The only item of note is that of £621 for working the destructors at the Electric Light Station trans- ferred by agreement from the Electricity Com- mittee to the Sanitary Committee. The estimated receipts for this year are £3,662 more than the last, I a sum having been added for sale of landsl; the sales ,1 of manure are more, and there are slight increases under other heads. In the Sewers Rate Account the expenditure is £125 less than list year, but we have an overdraft at the bank of £4l, as against £867 in hand last year. We shall therefore require £2,551 as against £1,777. (Hear, hear, and applause). I Alderman FAIRCLOUGH concluded by moving: (I) I That the Council hereby estimate the amount of .£35,298 Is. lid, will, in addition to the borough funcl,he required, and sudicient for the purposes to which the , borough fund is applicable, under the Municipal Cor- porations Act, 1882, or otherwise by law, for the year to end 31st March, 100 G. (2) That the Council do hereby order a borough rate to be made in pursuance of the Municipal Corporations Act 1892, in order to raise the said amount. (3) That the overseers of the township of Warrington be and they are hereby ordered to pay to the Treasurer of the borough, by instalments, and on of before such dates as may be fixed by the Finance and Estate Committee, the contribution of the sum or £35,298 Is. lid, out of the poor rate made or to be made for the said township of Warrington, as provided by the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882." Alderman BENNETT seconded. He pointed mit th a the amount estimated for the cleansing and flushing of sewers was only £3OO as against £450 last year. His impression was that the flushing was not carried on as satisfactorily as it ought to be.He did notlknow whether the recent fatality was due to that, but certainly the smell from some sewers was very cfiensive. The Cur poratiou ought, in his opinion, to spend more instead of less on that work. The only item which had been , deleted from the estimates was £2OO for branch libraries and in face of the vote of the Council earlier in the evening in favour of the libraries he would suggest the desirability of reinstating the amount in the budget. The Council agreed that the sum of £2OO for branch libraries should he inserted in the Borough rate and the resolution authorising the collection of £35,293 Is. 11d. in respect of that rate VMS carried unanimously. Alderman Rumor-of:oft then moved the confirmation of the estimate for an improvement rate of 3s. in the £ to be collected by two half-yearly instalments. The NIAYOR said municipal rates all over the country were going up by leaps and bounds, and instead of regarding it as " municipal extravagance and wilful waste." the blame should be pat on the right shoulders. The Governments which had been in °Mee had passed various Acts which Corporations had had to carry out ; for instance, the lVarrington Corporation had been landed in a sum of Is. Old. for the education rate, instead of a penny. The hospital cost nearly 6d. in the £ ; there used to be no municipal expenditure under that head. The cost of street lighting had increased,by 2d. in thee, as the system had to be put in a state of efficiency and the library cost another id. Thus they had nearly 2s. in the £ entailed by expenditure which was not necessary twenty or thirty years ago. If they had higher rates they expected to get value for their money. If the Governments would keep on passing Acts, and they must do this and that the responsibility for the extra expenditure should be placed on the right shoulders. So far as Corporations were concerned there was the Local Government Board to see that they were not guilty of wilful extravagance. Street improvement was an important branch of their work in Warrington. The town had been under the ban of narrow streets. It had cost them nearly 10d. in the £ to widen streets,and Ito put the town in a better and more sanitary condition. But they not only widened streets but got a better rateable value that would practically pay for the in- creased rate all over the town to make it up. When they widened a street and put a higher rateable value on property they obtained rates that should practically wine off the sinking fund. It was well it should be - understood that the rates in Warrington were higher through no fault of the Corporation, but through carry- ing out improvements and Acts of Parliament which had never been contemplated.

Councillor ST()TT said that the gentlemen who strongly objected to Municipal debt were the men who were greatly interested in certain financial concerns. That was proved at the Municipal Corporation's Association meeting by the Chairman. The rates would be lower next year, but they could not hope for some consider- able time that the rates would begin to seriously decrease in Warrington. He thought the Council and the Finance Committee were nrdzing a very serious mistake in purchasing land and then re-selling at-- The Tows CLERK : We are bound to sell surplus land.

div.head: Meeting in St. John's Ward.
div.p: Meeting in St. John's Ward.
- Protection and the Workingman. VIGOROUS SPEECH BY MR. H. VIVIAN. ----

There was a large and enthuslastio attendance at the second of the series of Liberal meetings which was held in the Wiuvrick street Co-operative Hall, on Wednesday evening. Mr. W Furness presided and was supported by Alderman Pierpoiut, Mr. H. Vivian, prospective candidate for the Birkenhead division, Mr. C. E. Parker, president of the Warrington Liberal Association Councillor Magi, nn :Ur. S. Wright, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes and Mr. A. Fish. The CIIAIRM AN said he thought the question of fiscal reform had so long occupied the attention of the country that we ought to be in a position to give judgment upon it. When we took the results of the bye-elections which had taken place during the past two years, from Bury to Brighton, he thought we would see that the country was without doubt in opposition to Mr. Chamberlain's policy.. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Furness proceeded to deal , with promises which Mr. Chamberlain had made, and never carried out. Referring to the question of old- age pensions, he said the country should undoubtedly ' provide means by which old men could live and end their days in contentment and peace.

OLD AGE PENSIONS would cost the country £10,000,000 a year and Mr. Chamberlain had excused the non-fulfilment of his promise by saying that the country was not in a position to spend that sum. Yet he spent £2,50.000,000 in further- ing the interests of the mining magnates in South Africa—enough money to provide old age pensions for the next twenty-five years. (Applause.) Dealing with the fiscal question and the statement that it was neces- sary to make an alteration in our fiscal ,policy in order to more closely unite us with the Colonies,he pointed out that we were already taxed to a large extent in favour of the Colonies and submitted that it would be injustice for us to be still further texed in their interest. (Haar, hear.) if the Colonies wanted to 1,6 drawn closer it could be easily done. We said to the Colonies "We take whatever goods you have to send free " and if the Colonies would only say the same and receive our goods under the same conditioes he thought the problem of closer union with the Colonies would be settled almost immediately. (Applause.) Mr. VIVIAN, who was cordially received, said that so far as he could see there had not, probably for the past century, been a political fight with issues more numerous or important. It was essential that the vital question of Protection versus Free Trade should not hang over the country for a number of years. It was diilicult to over-estimate the. cost in money alone to this country as a result of the uncertaintyof the question.(Applause.) In every protected country Protection was kept alive because it raised the cost of the commodity to the con- sumer. If the foreigner paid the taxes upon goods imported into England, as the fiscal reformers stated, why not tax everything and reduce our inperial taxes ? (Laughter.) The tariff reformers were quacks and jugglers and their case would not stand examination. (Applause). He asked them not to believe the silly nonsense that a nation could tax itself into prosperity. Free Trade brought the world's services to the door of the humblest worker. Under Free Trade,countries strove one against the other to give to the English labourer the biggest basket of goods for the .£1 which he earned weekly. Protectionists wanted to come between those countries and the labourerand they were willing to serve and take something out of the basket which he strove to fill with his bard earned money. (Applause.) Pro- tection was nothing more or less than LEGALIZED BRIGANDAGE. Workmen had been captured by Mr. Chamberlain who held before them advantages to their particular trade

but Mr. Chamberlain forgot to tell them that in order to fulfil his promise to benefit other industries the cost of living would be increased. In the long run it would be the man with • the lowest earning power and the lowest political power who would bear the burden of taxes and it was the workingman who would suffer as the result of Protection. (Applause.) Protection would not unite the empire but would lead to discord, as it would be practically impossible to establish a system of tariffs which would be equitable and which would lead to the maintaining of peace. Moreover, we had to consider not only the political empire, but also the commercial empire. We could not keep industry between four political walls. Protection would not unite but alienate the colonies,and would lead to corruption in our political life. The House of Com- mons would become the happy hunting ground of trust formers and financial magnates, and the moment we adopted Protection we would destroy the purity of our political life. There was not a single protected country in the world in which the Government was pure. (Applause).

_ _ WE WANTED GREATER EFFICIENCY, and wanted to get greater value for the money we spent. There had been no Government of modern times so wasteful and indifferent to economy as the present Government. Toryism lived by being bolstered up by groups of powerful industries. Maar, hear). Liberalism lived by placing the welfare of the people before any group however powerful. The question which the electors had to answer was as to whether or not political machinery was to be run in a manner which would promote the highest and best interests of the people,economically educationally and intellectually. (Applause). Mr. Vivian proceeded to refer to the auditors' report upon the South African War, pointing out how by the inefficiency of the Government, individuals supplying war stores had been able to escape the exact fulfilment of their contracts. "1 beg of you" he said in conclusion. 'not to allow a Government to be returned which has shown its alliance to industries rather than to Qv:, people, but to return a Government pledged to do something to take the politic tl machinery of this country out of the hands of these scoundrels, these fleecers, these sanpers of the people's wealth, and place it in the hands of people who will return to the old policy of peace, retrenchment and reform.' (Applause.) Councillor MAGINN, who was accorded a hearty recep- tion, used the present position of the glass trade as an illustration of the]fact that the adoption of Protection would increase thecost of living. Thestrike in Belgium had, be said, had the effect which a tariff would have as it had stopped the supply of Belgian glass. The result was that the price of glass had gone up about 15 per cent while the wages of the glass workers had not been altered. Continuing, he said

MR. PIERPOINT ABLY REPRESENTED BREWERS, SEMI- MILLIONAIRES AND LANDOWNERS in the district but had done nothing for the working- men who elected him. In the House of Commons he had done nothing to back up or introduce Bills which would be to the benefit of the working people of the country. It was said that this was going to be Mr. Pierpoint's last time in the House of Commons—(a voice "it is ")—and for that reason they were asked to vote for him and again return him so that he might be a comfortable warming pan to keep the seat ready for another Conservative. (Applause.) The present Government had tried to pass ait Aliens' Bill and pleaded as an excuse for not doing so that they were not strong enough, and yet fourteen days before, they were strong enough to pass a Bill allowing the introduction of Chinese labour into South Africa. (Applause.) Mr. Robert Pierpoint advocated a re-distribution Bill as it would reduce the representation of Ireland. That was the attitude taken up by a gentleman who asked them for their votes. He (the speaker) did not appeal to Irishmen but to every man of common honesty as to whether that was fair? (Applause). Mr. HowEs sail he thought Councillor Maginn would have been much stronger upon the Irish question. Personally he was a home ruler on principle and not upon policy, as he maintained every man had a right to govern himself. (Applause.) He could assure them that if a Liberal Government desired to to give home rule to Ireland they would do so openly and not secietly as the present Government were -doing. Ireland required better administration and it any man would only study the question the bogey of home rule would frighten him no longer, and the Irishman would be a poor soul who did not resent the scurrilous attempt on the part of the Tories to stir up race feeling and animosity. (Applause.) If the Tories tried to win an election by that cry he was sure the in- telligence of the people of Warrington would show itself by the return of the Liberal candidate. (Applause) The speakers were heartily thanked for their addresses, Mr. Vivian briefly responding. Mr. PARKER remarked that in Warrington they were not going to be frightened by the cry of home rule, and the Liberal party were not going to desert the Irish cause. (Applause). A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meet- ing.

div.head: GREAT RESERVOIR OE_TFIINGS
div.p: GREAT RESERVOIR OE_TFIINGS

from which we could draw at will, under tho Free • Trade system. "Mind "said Mr. Maddison, " that you keep the universe of God open to everything you want to buy, without a single handicap being placed upon the goods that may come in." Mr. Maddison quoted from • the Blue Book to show that the United Kingdom ex- ported 83 per cent, in manufactured goods ; Germany .61 per cent, and the United States, 22 per cent. Was not , that a triumph for Free Trade ?(Applanse).Mr. Maddison concluded with a stirring appeal to his hearers to resist t to the utmost the invasion of the Protectionist army. They would have

div.head: GIIFIA.T CTIANCE AT THE NEXT ELECTION
div.p: A GIIFIA.T CTIANCE AT THE NEXT ELECTION

in the town. They ii;ci-a-Ma-T;;:h;;i;o.d.i;i: the great priniples of Free imports, who understood what the meaning of raw material and food was, and he (Mr. Maddison) asked them to go to the poll remembering those worthies who in the past amid gloom, darkness and misery with great odds against them, forged on for freedom. When they had once again secured Free Trade, safe from the maurauding hands of Mr. Chamber- lain and his gang, they would go on, as Cobden bade them, and, having got free exchange in goods they would try to get free access to the land. (Applause). Mr. J. MORTON, secretary of the Progressive Labour League, addressed the meeting and spoke of the pro- gress which the League was making. The more they looked into the arguments of Protectionists the more ridiculous they appeared. ([fear, hear.) He hoped that ere long we would have Free Trade all round, but to attain it we must work in an amicable spirit with foreigners and colonials alike. He trusted that at the election Mr. Crosfield would be returned by such a majority as would make it certain that, so far as Warring- ton was concerned at any rate, the Protective policy had no chance whatever. (Applause). Mr. JO3EYIT HOWES, in moving a vote of thanks to the speakers, remarked that Mr. Chamberlain said he would not tax offal because it fed the pigs, but he would tax broad which fed human beings. The speaker strongly criticised the Government's action in sanctioning the introduction of Chinese labour in South Africa, and pointed out that according to the letter of a British officer in charge of one of the vessels conveying coolies to the Cape, the Chinese imported included

div.head: somi OF THE WORST CHARACTERS IN CHINA..
div.p: somi OF THE WORST CHARACTERS IN CHINA..

Referring to the recent strike of Chinese on the Rand, because the labourers were dissatisfied with the pay of is. per day, Mr. Howes said such events were degrading to our nation. Continuing, he said he honestly believed Toryism to be immorality in politics, and they must cleanse the country from it. The worst Liberal Govern- ment was as superior to the best Tory Government as daylight was to darkness. (Laughter and applause) The speech of Sir H Campbell Bannerman in the House on Wednesday night did him credit, and inspired the con- fidence of the nation. Sir Henry declared himself as firmly as ever in favour of giving the Irish the manage- ment of their own affairs. The Irish members showed that they appreciated his sincerity in the matter. It was time the problem was solved in order that it might not be used to serve the Tory party when they had no part of their policy which they dare defend. (Applause.) Mr. W. FURNESS seconded the vote of thanks which was heartily accorded. Mr. MADDISON responded and moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

Mr. MORTON seconded and said he was not altogether sorry the political aspect in the Council had taken such a turn. They now knew who they had to deal with and in future they would know how to tackle their opponents. The vote was unanimously passed. The CHAIRMAN, in acknowledging the compliment said he probably did not regret,after all, the turn events had taken with reference to local politics. It was per- haps just as well that they should have the declaration— which although it was not given in as many words was shown in actions—that in future politics should rule. In his opinion it was not desirable that a man should be sent to the Council simply because he was a Liberal or a Tory—it was not in his opinion,consuhing the best interests of the town—but it was as well that they should know what the opinion of the Conservatives was, and then at the proper time they would bo able to meet it. He was rather proud to have been the member over whose election the Pattie was fought, although it gave him a great deal orpersonal pain to see the action some men took in the matter. It would he a lesson as far as the Liberal party was concerned, and in future they must go for what was hest in the interest of War- rington only, aud make no compromise with Conserva- tives or anyone else. Then they would have a straight issue and a straight fight, and he bad no fear of the result. (Applause.)

div.p: PENNY BANKS.

A summary of the information with reference to Penny Saving Banks which had been obtained from the schools at which such banks are conducted in accord- ance with the decision of the committee at the meeting on the 23rd February, 1905, was submitted, and it was Resolved, that a copy of the circular upon the subject from the Board of Education be forwarded to ,the Managers of those schools at which such Bau.ks are not carried on, in the hope that the Managers may be able to see their way to their institution. _

div.head: KING'S SCITOLAIISHIP.
div.p: KING'S SCITOLAIISHIP.
A circular letter from the Board of Education, draw- ing attention to certain changes in the future arrange- ments for the King's Scholarship examinatian, was sub- mitted and noted.

The Rev. John Yonge and the• Director were appointed to represent the Committee upon the Council of the Society for University Extension in Liverpool and Dis- trict for the session 1905-G. THE ATTENDANCE OF CEITLDE.EN AT CHURCH At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee it was resolved that Mr. Councillor Luke Ellison be appointed chairman of the committee for the ensuing . .

A letter was submitted from the managers of the Heathside National school, intimating that the usual annual service commencing at 8.45 a.m. will be held ore I Ascenson Day in the St. Paul's Church,that the scholars will be back at school by 9.30 a.m., and that, as usual. arrangements will be made whereby any children whose parents may prefer it will receive secular instruction in the school whilst the others are at church.—After some discussion, it was resolved, that the managers of the school be informed that the committee have noted this intimation, and that they be reminded that permission should be obtained from the Education Committee when it is desired that a school should not be opened until a later hour than usual. ' It was resolved, that the year ended the 31st March, 1905, ,be counted as a year of service to Mr. William Rutter, assistant school attendance inspector, and that,. in accordance with the scale, his salary be increased !from 30s. to 325. 6d. per week, as from the Ist April, 1905.
--The action of the Rota Sub-Commitee in asking for information to be obtained as to the schools from which children attended church on Ash Wednesday, was confirmed.

THE NEW SCHOOLS. His Worship the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Bolton) was appointed Chairman of the Sites and Buildings Com- mittee for the ensuing year. Tt was decided to hold a special meeting of the Com- mittee at 4 o'clock on the afternoon of Friday, the 14th, April, for the purpose of considering the plans of the• "Bolton" and Beamont" Council schools,as amended to meet the Committee's requirements.

div.head: PHYLLIS THE ELUSIVE.
div.p: PHYLLIS THE ELUSIVE.

Chrysalis. [By Godfrey Dean.] " I like the twilight," Phyllis said—the room being- milighted—" It is suggestive. And in some moods artificial light is "—she shivered. There is in everyone (especially women) a sense of romance, more or less undeveloped, which, unless nourished in secret, is gradually stifled by the h realities of life.
" The half-light does leave- something to the imagi- nation," I said," but whence this mood ?".

"I don't know," she said, " exactly." Then, " saw a poet to-day. I could have loved a poet if "—she• paused, with dreamy eyes. " One permits a woman," I said, hastily and "With. an effort, to have a sentimental liking for a poet while loving someone else."

At my tone, which I could not altogether disguise, Phyllis looked up. " Bat you don't know him, do you ? " I do, I said, naming' him_ " His history is a tragedy—for a poet." " What is it ? " she asked. "I am interested." "It must begin," I said, " with the pretty romance. that surrounds the early life of the poet. But you can imagine it for yourself." Phyllis moved a little more into the shadow. "Tell it me," she insisted, so, not unwilling, I complied. "Life was full of promise. Was not the pathway he would tread alluringly lined with sweet flowers, for which he had but to reach out his hand? Poor lad! He knew not that many flowers are sweet only to the eye, and that the possessiOn of them often proves. a curse.

"He had yet to learn that the ability to discriminate' truly sometimes comes too late: youth's illusions! sacrificed at the altar of experience. "He was proud of the knowledge that he was gifted with seven talents, but he never questioned that they• would be rightly used. He dreamed of the world: gradually awakening to the beauty of his poesy. Some day he would journey to London, and all men should- laud his genius. " Such were his thoughts and the years came and went. His face grew more beautiful, the dark hair flowing in waves from his wide, white forehead. Men.,, stared at him ; women, passing him, smiled—some: unconsciously. But he was indifferent to these atten- tions, for with head erect, and unseeing eyes, he passecr.; strangers by, as though his mind were bent on some. great effort. " Some recognition of his powers he had had u;.,• enough to loose his fancy to farther flights. One dc he met a stranger—an old man—whom he directed toe' a distant part of the town. He had been in Londo.:. so long, said the stranger, that his native village had: grown out of his memory. " ' You have been to London,' asked the youth: eagerly. 'Ah, then -tell me something of it ! ' The old man's eyes scanned the pure lines of the lad's lac.. as the latter told of his desires and ambitions, but,' noting the weakness of the chin, he shook his head.:• ,Stay at home, my Lad, and content yourself; Londou'&:. not what it seems.' Nothing further would the olci man say." I was glad that Phyllis was looking very thoughtful-e' ' " The parable I am going to tell you now," I said. " is one of his, and I admire' it exceedingly, because it, is true to life, and was delicately and beautifully': 'expressed." She did not speak. " A summer's day. Full length on the grass, ha , sleeping, lay the dreamer. He had wandered away': from the busy streets, and, stretching himself on tbs., sward, given himself up to the peaceful surroundings. He lifted his head drowsily. A bird was sweepiaX ! near by, attracted to sonic object—so close was it he, could almost see the down beneath the wings. " It paused in the air, flew on, and, turning rapidly,. , alighted on the grass by a leaf, on which was a cater-, pillar. Protected by its colour likeness to the surroun&, ing vegetation the caterpillar would have escaped the; observation of the bird but for its proximity to some alien object. The lad raised his arm, and the startled., bird rose in the air, while the caterpillar crawl 4 away out of sight. His action was no idle impulse ;•0. yet he was hardly conscious of the thought that,- impelled it. 'I don't know why I (lid it,' he said, but —some day it will be a butterfly.' " Phyllis sighed lightly. Only her features were dig: ting,uishable now. "is that all " " The poet," I said, " expresses perfectly the highest; ideals of life. An ordinary man may do his duty, ber' unselfish, do graceful actions, have ambitions —k, short, live a noble life—and yet lack the gift 01'. expression. His life is a poem, for he lives it truly and he is a poet. Your poet's tragedy is the what-7 might-have-been. "Your sex loves the poet, for he , sings of thest; things, and of their ideals which struggle often fo . expression. The singing poet is to be honoured, but': do not forget that he does not necessarily embod); these virtues, and that the ordinary man may be 3 truer poet, though lacking the expression. The eate pillar in fact, is a potential butterfly, and I am ' caterpillar." "How serious you have been," she said ; "it is Ito ; like you." "Position dictates perspective and"— . I heard the soft rustle of her dress as she rose, and,' paused, amid then came forward to where I was, now' also standing., "I am sorrir," she said, "so very sorry." " but I did not mean that. I think it is ever so muc better that one should complete what one is going tc''' say," she gently suggested. " Women, almost solely, create cynics," I said. " Men sometimes invite it," she said, looking int°;', my eyes, and thus taking advantage of Inc. (Hosc: could Ibe expected to retain my firmness when near her ?) " I meant to say that I could have roved: a poet if you had been one." " You had better say butterfly now," I said. V " No. I would rather say Ido love a caterpf'lla• , It is nice even to be a caterpillar. , (To be continued.) (These articles originally appeared in the "London Echo.")

The questions of the appointment of road foreman was fully considered and it was resolved that the position be re- advertised at a commencing salary of 50s. per week, and that the person appointed be required to carry out the additional duties formerly performed by the road foreman of macadam roads. At a meeting on March 27th the committee considered 87 applications for the position of road foreman, and resolved that the follow- ing be requested to attend a special meeting of the committee :—Mr. Joseph Cook, Croft; Mr. J. Ilitton, Croft ; Mr. Joseph Marsh, Oldham. At a meating held on April 3rd,the committee interviewed the three candi- dates, and it was resolved that Mr. Cook be appointed road foreman'at a salary of 503. per week, the engage- ment to be terminated by 14 days' notice on eitber side. Alderman TINNION proposed the confirmation of the minutes. They had to regret the loss by death of John Smith, their macadam road foreman, who was a very good servant, and they felt they had lost a good man. Referring to the unfortunate accident which occurred in the sewer in Ellesmere-street, he wished to say how deeply the committee regrettted the occurrence, and how deeply they sympathised with the widow and chil- dren of James l3fitxter. As to the legal responsibility he had nothing to say. That would be the subject of litigation. The committee had their attention called to the very heroic conduct of John Stockton, who at great risk and danger went down the sewer and to a very considerable extent helped to save the lives of several other men who most assuredly would have been suffocated if it had not been for his pluck. (Hear, hear.) The committee decided to vote the sum of £lO as some slight recompense for him, and in some way to mark their sense of his heroic conduct. As to the ques- tion of the road foreman, the committee decided owing to the death of the macadam road foreman to re-ad vet tise for this position and to give an increase of 10s. per lweek in the hope of getting a superior man and he did I not hesitate to say they had in Mr. Cook got a better man than any who applied on the last occasion. Councillor ROBERTS seconded. Councillor STorr said in taking the names of the men who were unemployed in the to /an they found that a large proportion were connected with the paving and sewerage trade. He urged that any new road repairing work should be pushed forward as soon as possible, in order to find work for these men. The MAYOR observed that in reference to the hmic conduct of Stockton he might say that the Shipwreck and Humane Society of Liverpool had decided to grant him a silver medal and an illuminated address, and had asked him (the Mayor) to make the presentation, which he had promised to do. Councillor CLEGG supported the minutes, and said he thought the services of the men who rendered such valuable assistance in restoring animation should be recognized. He was on the spot a few minutes afterthe accident, and it was the unanimous opinion of every- body that these men worked splendidly. He would like to suggest that the thanks of the Council be presented to these men who rendered first aid. The MAYOR said Councillor Clegg could not add to the minutes. hut Alderman Tionion would doubtless

UNPROTECTED FiRES. Burning Fata!ity at Warrington. • Another illustration of the danger arising from the unfortunately for too common practice of leaving children in a room in which there is an unprotected fire, was afforded at Warrington, on Friday of last week. On that day the wife of Samuel Ball, 3, Carlisle-street, according to the statement she made on Monday,left her house whilst she went to a shop a few door away. She took her little son, aged three years, with her, but when in the shop she missed him, and later was informed he had been badly burned and taken to the Infirmary. There was no guard or fender in front of the kitchen fire at the time. Mr. Duffey, a man who lodges with Mr. Ball, spoke to seeing the lad's clothing in flames. He extinguished the flames. Deceased's sister said her brother was trying to get some potatoes out of a pan on the fire when his clothing caught fire. The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death." Mr. S. Brighouse, the coroner, said he did not know what was going to he done. It was only what parents I could expect if they left young children in a house in which were unprotected fires. The fact that there was in that case a pan on the fire made things more dangerous, as eery child tried to see what a pan Con- tained. Perhaps in &omit 25 years legislature would step in, but the House of Commons did not move quickly,and required stirring up. The Prince of Wales, in his new capacity as Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, has been pleased to accept a copy of Mrs. Stepney Rawson s "Tales of Rye Town," which bas just been published by Messrs. Archibald Constable & Co.

The money is to he invpsted and paid to the boy's aunt at the rate of six shillings a week.
